title: $2.145M 5-year debenture for the Elmdale/Lumber reconstruction at 2.4%
summary: By-law 2061 borrowed $2.145M over 5 years from the Royal Bank of Canada at 2.4% to fund most of the 2015 Elmdale Street and Lumber Avenue reconstruction (a local improvement). Council stressed it was budgeted, would not change the tax rate, and came in under what was expected.
status_detail: First and second reading Dec 15, 2015 (Siemens moved; second reading by Councillor 'Pootmans' [unclear]/Zwaagstra); Municipal Board approved; third reading Feb 2, 2016.
figures: $2.145M debenture, 2.4% over 5 years vs 7% projected (transcript 2015-12-15, 0:12:41 and 0:13:46).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: only a 5-year term, 'as is our normal' (Jac Siemens)
notes: Third reading on Feb 2, 2016 (0:15:14) is described by staff; mover there not clearly identified.

title: Barkman Avenue renewal: $2.1M local improvement with $1M borrowed over 5 years
summary: Local Improvement Plan 2016-01 rebuilt three blocks of Barkman Avenue (surface, water and sewer mains) for about $2.14M: $1M borrowed over 5 years, $840k from the Canada-Manitoba Infrastructure Program and $300k from the Municipal Road Improvement Fund. Council said it was the only new debt in 2016 and would not raise the tax rate. One objection was registered; no one spoke at the hearing.
status_detail: First and second reading Dec 15, 2015; Municipal Board approved; third reading Feb 16, 2016 (moved by Zwaagstra, seconded by a Councillor Penner). The work was done in 2016 and the $1M debt by-law 2074 got first and second reading Dec 20, 2016 at 2.33% over 5 years.
figures: $2.14M total; $1M debt (5 years); $840k Canada-Manitoba Infrastructure Program; $300k MRIF (2015-12-15, 0:06:22). Borrowing rate 2.33%/yr for 5 years (2016-12-20, 0:36:43).
reasons: infrastructure-first: infrastructure renewal continues to be a priority (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: partnership with provincial and federal governments gets more done (Mayor Chris Goertzen)
public: One registered objection to the local improvement (named in the council package; not read out). No one spoke at the Dec 15, 2015 public hearing.
vote: carried; 'Opposed?' called on first reading, none audible
notes: The objector's name is not given in the transcript.

title: Supplementary taxes beat budget ($1.3M vs $750k); 2017 interim budget passed
summary: On Dec 6, 2016 council accepted just over $1.3M in supplementary taxes on new construction, well above the $750,000 budgeted. Zwaagstra said this frees money for the 2017 budget. Council also passed the routine 2017 interim operating budget (the financial plan comes in late January or February) and renewed the RBC overdraft authority.
status_detail: Supplementary taxes accepted (Dec 15, 2015 and Dec 6, 2016); interim budget carried Dec 6, 2016 (Zwaagstra moved, Siemens seconded).
figures: 2016 supplementary taxes just over $1.3M vs $750k budgeted (2016-12-06, 0:04:10 and 0:05:11); the Feb 2016 hearing had projected $700k.
notes: Projected figure was $700k at the Feb hearing and $750k per staff in December.

title: Province shifts Dutch elm disease costs: about $20,000 a year more for the city
summary: The province moved its Dutch elm disease program funding to municipalities without the capital costs, leaving Steinbach about $20,000 a year more to pay. Council signed the new agreement to keep protecting its elms and agreed to send the Minister of Conservation a letter of frustration.
status_detail: Agreement approved Jan 19, 2016; letter to the minister agreed by consensus.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: province downloaded program without capital costs (Mayor Chris Goertzen)

title: Performing arts centre: $7.5M city cap, $22.5M grant application
summary: Council kept the performing arts centre as the first phase of recreation renewal. A task force (both Councillors Penner and Zwaagstra) reported on Mar 15 that the business plan showed a $500,000–600,000 yearly operating deficit and urged council to secure funding first. On Sep 6 council approved a Small Communities Fund application for a $22.5M project: the city's $7.5M plus $7.5M each sought from the federal and provincial governments.
status_detail: Application approved Sep 6, 2016 (moved by a councillor, seconded by Fehr; carried). Funding was not confirmed in 2016; by December the class C estimate was $24.3M (see 2016-pac-reaffirm-sunset).
figures: City share $7.5M (cap set July 2015); application total $22.5M (2016-09-06, 1:20:56); PAC operating deficit $500k–$600k/yr (2016-03-15, 0:26:16); provincial $5M commitment letters to the first phase noted Jan 19, 2016.
reasons: partner-money: solidify funding before any other moves (Councillor Penner (task force))
notes: Mover on Sep 6 (label B) not named.

title: Residents' request for an Old Tom Road sidewalk ($700–800k) left out of the paving project
summary: Two Lyons Gate residents (surname initial T.) asked for a sidewalk with the Old Tom Road paving. Staff said their cost estimate of $700,000–800,000 would roughly double the $1M set aside. Council members said sidewalks should be weighed in the city's overall sidewalk program, not added to boundary-road paving.
status_detail: Taken as information; council said it would be considered in the overall sidewalk and pathway plan. No sidewalk was added to the 2016 project.
figures: Sidewalk $700k–$800k vs $1M budgeted for the project (staff, 2016-02-02, 1:19:50).
reasons: infrastructure-first: focus on the roadway first; sidewalks are a separate discussion (Jac Siemens); ability-to-pay: would virtually double the paving budget (Unidentified councillor)
public: Two Lyons Gate residents (T.) wrote asking for a sidewalk along Old Tom Road.
notes: Residents' first names not given; identified by surname initial only. The 1:20:44 speaker who urged not to 'conflate' paving and sidewalks is not named.

title: Curbside garbage special service renewed 2016–2018 with $10 in increases
summary: By-law 2059 and Special Service Plan 2016-1 continued residential curbside waste collection for 2016–2018, with the charge rising $3 in 2016, $3 in 2017 and $4 in 2018. One objection was registered and considered by the Municipal Board, which approved the plan.
status_detail: Third reading carried Feb 16, 2016 (moved by Siemens, seconded by Zwaagstra), after Municipal Board approval.
figures: +$3 (2016), +$3 (2017), +$4 (2018) = $10 over 3 years (transcript 0:08:08); solid waste cost ~$2.2M funded by user fees (financial plan hearing).
public: One registered objection (considered by the Municipal Board; objector not named).
notes: The debate remark at 0:08:08 is merged into the mayor's turn by the transcript and is garbled, so it is not quoted.

title: 2016 financial plan adopted: mill rate cut to 13.23 for a 'net zero' reassessment year
themes: budget; mill-rate; reassessment; debt; capital-plan; utility-rates; fees; process
summary: At the Feb 16, 2016 public hearing City Treasurer Brian Hrehirchuk presented a $27M operating plan and a $12.9M capital program. The municipal mill rate fell 1.07 mills to 13.23 to offset a roughly 16% reassessment increase, so the city took in no extra tax from existing properties; water and sewer rates rose about 4.8% and 1.6%, with small increases to residential garbage collection, land-use application and permit fees. No member of the public spoke. Council adopted the plan in principle the same day and formally on Apr 5, 2016, once school tax figures were in.
status_detail: Adopted in principle Feb 16, 2016 (moved by Zwaagstra, carried with no opposition called) and formally on Apr 5, 2016 (moved by Zwaagstra; carried). The PSAB-format version was passed Jun 21, 2016 (moved by Funk, seconded by Zwaagstra).
figures: Municipal mill rate 13.23, down 1.07 from 2015; property tax $13.8M; revenues just over $27M; capital program $12.9M ($6.6M new, $6.1M renewal, $150k studies); water +4.8%, sewer +1.6%; average home ~$195,000 → about $1,160 city tax; supplementary taxes $700k; per-capita provincial grant $2.145M, federal gas tax $730k, municipal programs grant ~$210k; labour $7.5M; police and fire ~$3.1M; new debt $1M (Barkman only), $2.76M repaid, year-end debt $7.6M, average rate ~2.6%, debt payments $3M = 2.54 mills (~19% of the city rate); school taxes just over half of a typical bill; 2017 capital program estimated at $17.4M (all from the Feb 16, 2016 hearing transcript, 0:01:21).
reasons: ability-to-pay: net zero reassessment budget: no tax increase while still renewing infrastructure (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: basic infrastructure 'always a top priority' (Barkman, overlays) (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: capital projects done in partnership with provincial and federal governments (Mayor Chris Goertzen); pay-as-you-go: 5-year amortization on all debt for lower interest (Brian Hrehirchuk (City Treasurer))
public: No member of the public spoke or asked questions at the hearing; the mayor noted a few people had come to the open house earlier that day.
vote: carried; no opposition called (Feb 16 and Apr 5)
notes: Seconder at the Feb 16 hearing was not audible. 'Steinbach' appears in the treasurer's slides wording in the transcript. Speaker F at 0:19:06 could not be identified.

title: Council asks Hanover School Division to consider freezing school taxes in 2016
summary: Councillor Earl Funk moved that the city formally ask Hanover School Division to consider a 2016 tax freeze, noting school taxes are about 55% of the tax bill while the city held the line. Councillor Jac Siemens agreed with the intent but said he would vote against a formal letter sent before meeting with the division. The mayor said Steinbach had the lowest taxes of any Manitoba city and that the request was appropriate.
status_detail: Carried Feb 16, 2016 ('Opposed?' was called; Siemens had said he would vote against). The mayor said he would follow up in person; no response from the division was recorded in 2016 transcripts.
figures: School taxes ~55% of the tax bill (Funk, citing the treasurer; transcript 0:17:34); no city tax increase since 2012 (Funk).
reasons: already-low-taxes: lowest taxes of any Manitoba city; Winkler next, about 17% higher (mayor's unverified estimate) (Chris Goertzen); ability-to-pay: leave more money in consumers' pockets to spur development (Earl Funk); provincial-responsibility: system flawed; school divisions should collect their own taxes (Unidentified councillor)
vote: carried; Siemens stated he would vote against
notes: The mayor's Winkler comparison ('don't quote me on it') is unverified.

title: 2015 year-end: ~$300k surplus to reserves, including $350k committed expenditure reserve
summary: Council approved the 2015 reserve transfers, including $350,000 to a committed expenditure reserve. Part of that ($50,000) was for a future tax-sharing payment to the RM of Hanover, funded from 2015 surplus. Zwaagstra stressed that reserves are a key source for capital programs. Reserves opened 2015 at about $12.5M.
status_detail: Carried Mar 15, 2016 (Zwaagstra moved, a Councillor Penner seconded). The preliminary 2015 statement got interim approval the same day, pending audit.
figures: Reserve opening balance 2015 ~$12.5M (0:48:02); $350k to committed expenditure reserve, incl. $50k for RM of Hanover tax-sharing (0:45:50); 2015 surplus available ~$300k (2016-05-03, 0:07:53).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: keep money in reserves for capital projects (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: The transcript garbles part of the $350k/$50k description ('Alderman Chabot'), so the split is uncertain.

title: $2.955M 2016 capital works tender (Barkman, pavement management, sidewalks)
summary: Council awarded the 2016 capital works tender of $2.955M to Maple Leaf Construction, about 10% under the estimate and within the $3.6M budget. It was funded from the gas tax reserve, the capital development reserve, debt and a Building Canada Fund grant.
status_detail: Carried Mar 15, 2016.
figures: Tender $2.955M; budget just under $3.6M (2016-03-15, 0:05:40).
reasons: infrastructure-first: proactive resurfacing avoids bigger costs later (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: 0.5% business tax continued; proceeds go to the Chamber of Commerce
summary: Council renewed the 0.5% business tax levy (By-law 2063). In December staff confirmed the ongoing arrangement under which business taxes, less 5% for collection, go to the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce. Core grant decisions like this one are made in the annual financial plan.
status_detail: First and second reading Apr 5, 2016; third reading May 3, 2016 (Zwaagstra moved).
figures: 0.5% business tax (2016-04-05 part 2, 0:35:07); chamber receives business taxes less 5% collection (2016-12-06, 0:17:09).
public: Steinbach Chamber of Commerce (organization) submitted its annual grant request letter and financial statements.

title: Four downtown lots bought for ~$1.12M from operating funds and reserves
summary: Continuing a roughly 20-year land assembly strategy near the T.G. Smith Centre and arenas, council bought 376 Hanover ($205,000, Apr 5), 385 Elmdale ($355,000, Sep 20), 316 Hanover ($230,000, Oct 18) and 326 Hanover ($331,200, Nov 1), paid from the general operating fund and reserves. Councillor Siemens opposed the April purchase, saying the city was taking starter homes off the market with no plan in place.
status_detail: All four purchases carried; Siemens stated opposition to the Apr 5 purchase ('Opposed?' called).
reasons: dont-burden-future: long-term strategy so land is available for future recreation or parking (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Siemens' opening words at 0:29:45 ('I won't vote I'm in favor of the motion') are garbled; his reasoning is clearly against.

title: Motion to drop the multiplex as unaffordable and keep 1.241 mills for the recreation reserve
summary: A Councillor Penner moved recreation-planning principles: a multiplex is 'not financially feasible', the performing arts centre goes ahead downtown only with other-government funding, at least 10% of its capital must be raised privately, land is sought for a future arena outside downtown, and 1.241 mills a year keep going to the recreation reserve. Seconder Michael Zwaagstra said a $71–100M multiplex was impossible on $13M a year of tax revenue. Mayor Goertzen opposed, saying council was abandoning its master plan just as federal infrastructure money was opening up.
status_detail: Carried 5-2 (against: Mayor Goertzen, John Fehr), per SteinbachOnline; the video ends before the vote. Council then proceeded on an arts-centre-first basis with a capped $7.5M city share.
figures: Multiplex estimates: MNP 2012 over $100M; Stantec 2014 about $71M; city property-tax revenue ~$13M/yr; recreation reserve levy 1.241 mills ≈ $1.1M/yr; borrowing $33M over 20 years ≈ $2.5M/yr debt payment (2016-04-05 part 2, 0:45:52–0:50:47).
reasons: ability-to-pay: $13M tax base cannot carry multiplex financing or operating costs without massive tax increases (Councillor Penner (Cari or Susan; first name not determined)); ability-to-pay: even two-thirds grant funding leaves $33M of debt and a tax increase (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: PAC only with other-government money and 10% private (Councillor Penner (Cari or Susan; first name not determined)); study-first: (against the motion) finish the master plan first; take a couple more months (Chris Goertzen)
notes: Speaker labels in this video are unstable (Zwaagstra's speech is split across labels G, M and B); only the 0:49:25 turn right after he is called is used. Which Penner moved is not stated; Zwaagstra on Mar 15, 2016 named both Susan and Cari Penner as task-force members. Vote and mover from SteinbachOnline ("A complex history of Steinbach's multiplex"; "Penner wants to drop arts centre plan").

title: Old Tom Road paving: $200k overrun covered from surplus or reserve rather than cutting scope
summary: The Old Tom Road paving tender came in about $200,000 over its $1M budget. On Apr 5 council tabled staff's reduced-scope option at Councillor Siemens' request. On May 3 council awarded the full tender to Bituminex, with the extra paid from the year-end surplus or, failing that, the capital development reserve.
status_detail: Tabled Apr 5 (Siemens moved, Fehr seconded); full tender awarded May 3 (Zwaagstra moved, Fehr seconded; carried).
figures: Low tender $1,058,417 + ~$140k engineering, ~ $200k over the $1M budget (2016-04-05 part 2, 0:23:44); capital development reserve to fall to about $500k; 2015 surplus ~$300k (2016-05-03, 0:04:37 and 0:07:53).
reasons: infrastructure-first: long-overdue road; should not delay or reduce scope again (Michael Zwaagstra); reserves-low: reserve would drop lower than recent years but still enough (Michael Zwaagstra); ability-to-pay: no tax rise this year, so extra dollars are hard to find (Mayor Chris Goertzen)

title: Water and sewer rate by-law for 2017 onward sent to the Public Utilities Board (~3% increases)
summary: Water and sewer rates, set about 3.5 years earlier, were due to expire at the end of 2016. Council gave first reading to By-law 2064 with increases of about 3% and sent it to the Public Utilities Board for review. Zwaagstra said rates must cover operations and future upgrades. The mayor said regular reviews avoid large catch-up increases.
status_detail: First reading carried May 17, 2016 (Zwaagstra moved, a Councillor Penner seconded); PUB approval and further readings were not found in the 2016 transcripts.
figures: Increases 'approximately in the range of 3%' (Zwaagstra, 0:06:18); 2016 plan increases water +4.8%, sewer +1.6% (Feb 16 hearing); utility operating cost ~$3.1M.
reasons: pay-as-you-go: rates must cover operating and future upgrades (Michael Zwaagstra); dont-burden-future: systematic reviews avoid large increases that are hard to absorb (Mayor Chris Goertzen)
public: Staff expected a PUB paper-notice process rather than a hearing, as past public concern was 'extremely minimal'.
notes: Final 2017 rates not found in this period's transcripts.

title: City Hall addition tendered at $1.44M after years of deferral
summary: Council awarded the City Hall addition to Penco Construction for about $1.44M, including roof resurfacing, under budget. Councillor Fehr noted it had been delayed several times for lack of funds.
status_detail: Carried Jun 21, 2016 (Fehr moved, a Councillor Penner seconded); construction to start mid-July 2016.
reasons: pay-as-you-go: deferred until funds were available (John Fehr)

title: Council expense policy updated (meal allowances)
summary: Council adopted minor updates to the council expense policy, mainly meal allowances adjusted for inflation, plus the matching employee expense policy. The policy is reviewed about every four years.
status_detail: Carried Jun 21, 2016 (moved by a Councillor Penner, seconded by the other Councillor Penner).
notes: Council indemnities (pay) were not debated in this period's transcripts.

title: Proposed annual dog licence fee (+$15) sent back for more work
summary: Staff proposed replacing the lifetime dog licence with an annual one costing $15 more, raising about $5,200 a year. Half would offset the roughly $33,000 animal control cost and half would go to a reserve, possibly for a dog park. Zwaagstra, Fehr and a Councillor Penner objected to raising fees without a specific project, and council sent it back to administration.
status_detail: Referred back to administration and possibly study session (consensus). No fee change found in 2016.
figures: Revenue ~$1,000/yr vs ~$33,000 animal control cost; proposed revenue ~$5,200/yr; altered dog from $10 lifetime to $25/yr (2016-06-21, 0:23:57 and 0:34:00).
reasons: ability-to-pay: pets are companionship for people who can't afford much else (John Fehr); study-first: name a specific benefit (e.g., dog park) and get feedback first (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: $10M water supply expansion: design awarded, 75% sought from other governments
summary: Council awarded AECOM the design of a new northwest water supply plant ($350,470 plus expenses). It then backed applications to the federal Clean Water and Wastewater Fund and the province for a $10M project: $5M federal, $2.5M provincial and $2.5M city.
status_detail: Design awarded Jun 21, 2016; funding resolutions passed Sep 6 and Oct 18, 2016. Funding approval not recorded in 2016.
reasons: partner-money: can only proceed with federal/provincial partners (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: adequate supply for the medium and long term (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Golf club asks for a $50,000/yr grant and help with flood costs
summary: The Steinbach golf course board (spokesperson J.S.) asked for a water-management partnership, compensation for flood costs (about $48,000 a year in lost revenue), future damage funding and a $50,000-a-year recreational grant. It pointed to Winkler's $50,000-a-year support for its golf club. The mayor said the requests would go through the budget process ending in November. Councillor Fehr asked whether the province should pay, since the creek is a provincial drain.
status_detail: Referred to the budget process; no decision found in 2016 transcripts.
figures: Requested $50,000/yr grant; ~$48,000/yr lost revenue from closures (2016-07-05, 0:35:12–0:36:01); Winkler golf club $50,000/yr for 5 years (delegation's comparison).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: water runs through a provincial drain (John Fehr); study-first: deal with it in the budget process (Chris Goertzen)
public: Golf course board spokesperson J.S. made the requests; Winkler comparison is the delegation's claim (not verified).

title: Susan Penner: Steinbach taxpayers carry regional facilities' deficits
summary: In her Sep 20, 2016 opening remarks, Councillor Susan Penner said Steinbach serves 30,000–60,000 people on a tax base of about 15,000. Taxes from new businesses go to the infrastructure growth requires, and mostly non-resident users leave Steinbach taxpayers covering the aquatic centre's deficit, as they would the performing arts centre's. She asked whether the city could partner with surrounding RMs on regional facilities.
status_detail: A question raised for council's perspective; no motion or follow-up recorded in 2016.
figures: Population ~15,000; service region 30,000–60,000 (opening remarks, 0:00:01).
reasons: growth-pays: new property taxes are absorbed by the infrastructure costs of growth (Susan Penner); ability-to-pay: decisions must 'do right by Steinbach taxpayers' (Susan Penner)

title: Report requested on an Albert Street sidewalk for possible 2017 budget
summary: A resident asked for a sidewalk on Albert Street. Staff explained that sidewalks in older neighbourhoods were historically 50/50: half from benefiting owners and half from debt across the city. New neighbourhoods get sidewalks through development fees. Council asked for a cost report so it could be considered for the 2017 budget.
status_detail: Motion for a report carried Oct 4, 2016; no report found in 2016 transcripts.
figures: 50/50 local-improvement formula (staff, 0:20:10).
reasons: study-first: get information first; gauge owners' support if a cost share applies (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: A resident (correspondence) asked for a sidewalk and offered to canvass the street.
notes: Mover (label D) not named; resident not named in the transcript.

title: Development fees renewed for 2017–2019 at +2.5% a year
summary: Council renewed the residential (By-law 2070) and non-residential (By-law 2071) capital development fees for three years to the end of 2019, rising 2.5% a year. Zwaagstra said new development should pay toward its impact (sidewalks, transportation, fire services) while increases stay near inflation for affordability.
status_detail: First reading Oct 4, 2016; second and third reading Nov 1, 2016 (residential: Zwaagstra moved, Siemens seconded; third reading Siemens/Penner; non-residential: Fehr/Funk, then Funk/Siemens). All carried.
figures: +2.5% per year, 2017–2019 (2016-10-04, 0:11:07); 2016 plan expected $769k in capital development fees (Feb 16 hearing).
reasons: growth-pays: new developments contribute to the cost of their impact (Michael Zwaagstra); ability-to-pay: increase kept near inflation for affordability (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Haven Group asks for a development fee rebate for 55+ housing
summary: The Haven Group asked for a development fee rebate for a 55+ housing expansion. Staff said the city's past seniors housing grant was only for provincially approved assisted-living or supportive housing. Zwaagstra warned that funding ordinary 55+ housing would open a new and costly category. Council asked the group to clarify whether the project includes supportive housing.
status_detail: Council agreed by consensus to write back with the program criteria and wait for the Haven Group's reply; no decision recorded in 2016.
reasons: fairness-precedent: grant for regular 55+ housing could open the door to much other housing (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Haven Group (organization) letter requesting the rebate.

title: After a $24.3M estimate, council reaffirms its $7.5M PAC share with a June 30, 2017 deadline
summary: A class C estimate of $24.3M for the performing arts centre was released to the media before any council meeting, and some councillors publicly questioned the project. On Dec 20 Mayor Goertzen asked council to honour past votes. A motion reaffirmed the $7.5M city commitment, provided the other conditions were met, with a sunset date of June 30, 2017. Zwaagstra, Funk and a Councillor Penner opposed: the project was about 60% above the roughly $15M outer limit when the cap was set.
status_detail: Carried Dec 20, 2016 ('Opposed?' called); the commitment would lapse June 30, 2017 if the other funding wasn't in place.
figures: City share $7.5M (max 50% of a ~$15M project, July 2015 motion by Zwaagstra); class C estimate $24.3M (2016-12-20, 0:44:53).
reasons: ability-to-pay: estimate ~60% above the outer limit council worked with (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: city share stays $7.5M; if outside money doesn't come, the project dies anyway (John Fehr)
notes: No minutes; the vote count isn't stated. Likely 4-3 if the mayor and Speaker I (probably Siemens, who raised the point of order) voted for it, but unconfirmed.

title: City grants: $887,372 in 2017, nearly all to four large organizations
summary: Council's yearly grant reconciliation shows a focused policy: in 2017 the Jake Epp Library ($327,315), Steinbach Development Corporation ($239,655), Steinbach Arts Council ($152,705), Chamber of Commerce ($115,297, the business tax passed through) and Mennonite Heritage Village ($50,000) received almost all of $887,372; nine small groups got $200–$350 each. The business tax stayed at 0.5% and is passed to the Chamber.
status_detail: 2016 grants reconciliation accepted Feb 21, 2017; 2017 grants accepted unanimously Mar 20, 2018 (R18-065). In June 2018 Councillors Susan Penner and Funk called for more flexibility in the grants policy (see 2018-arts-centre-matching-grant).
figures: 2017 grants $887,371.78: Jake Epp Library $327,315; Steinbach Development Corporation $239,655.24; Chamber of Commerce $115,296.54; Mennonite Heritage Village $50,000; Steinbach Arts Council $152,705; Youth For Christ, Alternative Justice Committee, Community Foundation, Kidsport, South Eastman Rotary, Haven Group Foundation, Eden Foundation, Today House and South Eastman Filipino Association $200–$350 each ($2,400 total) (minutes R18-065). Business tax 0.5% (2018-04-17 0:13:48).
reasons: fairness-precedent: A 'simplified and focused' policy rather than case-by-case operating grants. (Chris Goertzen); capital-not-operating: Likes the policy's commitment to capital grants rather than operating grants. (Earl Funk)
public: The Pat Porter Active Living Centre called the select-organizations policy favoritism (Feb 2018).
notes: The Chamber amount equals the business tax collected and passed through, per Fehr (2017-03-21) and Zwaagstra (2018-04-17).

title: 2017 financial plan: mill rate up 0.7 mill to 13.93 to pay for the RCMP cost jump
themes: budget; mill-rate; policing-cost; debt; capital-plan; school-tax
summary: The 2017 plan raised the municipal mill rate by 0.7 mill to 13.93, and staff said all of the new revenue would pay for the city's larger RCMP share (70% to 90%) after the population passed 15,000. The $24.6M capital program included the proposed Performing Arts Centre and the supplementary water supply. Council approved the plan in principle at the Feb 21 hearing and gave the 2017 tax levy by-law (By-law 2078) first and second reading on Mar 21; Councillors Zwaagstra and Funk opposed the plan because of the arts centre and its borrowing.
status_detail: Approved in principle on Feb 21, 2017 (voice vote, carried). Tax levy By-law 2078 received first and second reading on Mar 21, 2017 (Zwaagstra against). Third reading is not in the available record: the Apr 4, 2017 video could not be downloaded and there are no 2017 minutes.
figures: Municipal mill rate 13.93, up 0.7 mill from 2016; revenues just over $28.5M; property taxes $14.8M ($13.5M from the mill rate), 51.7% of revenue; assessment growth about 1.9%; capital program $24.6M; new debt $5M, $2.5M repaid, debt about $10M at year end, average interest just over 2.5%; debt payments $2.8M = 2.3 mills (16.5% of the city rate); average house just under $200,000 pays just over $100/month in city tax; supplementary taxes $500K; provincial per capita grant $2.36M, federal gas tax $730K, municipal programs grant $210K; residential garbage about +2% (3-year rate plan); land-use and permit fees about +2.5%; no water or sewer increase proposed; labour $8M; protective services $3.8M (all from Brian Hrehirchuk's presentation, 2017-02-21 hearing 0:00:49).
reasons: policing-cost: The increase was forced by the RCMP cost share rising once the population passed 15,000; otherwise the budget was frugal. (John Fehr); growth-pays: Growth costs are normally covered by new assessment; the RCMP jump (a 30% increase) was the exception needing 0.7 mill. (Jac Siemens); dont-burden-future: Voted against: the arts centre borrowing would raise borrowing costs and take money from other needs. (Earl Funk); dont-burden-future: Voted against: could not support a plan whose largest capital item was a $24M arts centre, though it did not yet affect the mill rate. (Michael Zwaagstra); provincial-responsibility: On the tax levy by-law: the Hanover School Division increase is set by the division and the city must collect it. (Jac Siemens)
public: No one from the public spoke at the hearing, although the mayor noted it was the largest audience at a financial plan hearing in some time.
mover: a Councillor Penner (not identifiable from the video)
vote: carried by voice vote; Zwaagstra and Funk stated they would vote against (counts not recorded)
notes: No 2017 minutes exist; decisions and movers come from the transcripts. The mover of approval in principle is heard only as 'Councillor Penner'. The prior (2016) mill rate is not stated beyond 'up 0.7 of a mill'.

title: Performing Arts Centre: $7.5M city share ($5M to be borrowed) dropped when the funding deadline passed
summary: The proposed $24M downtown Performing Arts Centre was the largest item in the 2017 capital budget. The city's committed share was $7.5M: $5M from a future borrowing by-law and $2.5M from the recreation reserve, with the rest to come from other governments and donors. Council applied to the federal Canada Cultural Spaces Fund on Feb 21, 2017 (Zwaagstra against). When the June 30, 2017 deadline for all funding passed, the mayor announced the project would not proceed in its present form.
status_detail: The June 30, 2017 funding deadline (set in December 2016) was missed. On July 4, 2017 Mayor Goertzen said the project would not move forward in its present form and council would consult on future recreation and culture plans while still setting aside over $1M a year in the recreation and culture reserve. The planned borrowing never happened.
figures: $24M project, $12M budgeted in each of 2017 and 2018, $2.5M borrowing in 2017 (Zwaagstra, 2017-02-21 hearing 0:16:03); city commitment $7.5M = $5M debt + $2.5M recreation reserve (Warkentin, 2017-03-07 0:20:36); recreation reserve just over $750K at end of 2016, annual recreation levy about $1.1M (2017-03-07 0:19:35, 0:21:54); city operating-cost estimate about $80 per residential unit vs. $45 in a supporters' brochure (2017-03-07 0:23:02).
reasons: partner-money: The project depended on other funders; it stopped when all funding was not in place by June 30. (Chris Goertzen); dont-burden-future: Too large: 'the numbers just simply don't add up' even with a $5M federal grant. (Michael Zwaagstra); dont-burden-future: Opposed the borrowing; later called the cost 'massively inflated' and the process too closed. (Earl Funk)
public: In March 2017 a supporters' brochure said $7.5M was already in the recreation reserve and estimated operating costs at about $45 per household; council members pointed out the reserve held about $750K and the city's own estimate was about $80. In July 2017 resident T.M. asked whether '$5 million in a reserve fund' freed by the missed deadline could pay for the water project; the mayor said that money had been a future borrowing that never took place.
mover: a Councillor Penner (federal grant application, Feb 21, 2017)
vote: grant application carried; Zwaagstra stated he voted against
notes: The December 2016 resolutions that set the $7.5M commitment and the June 30 deadline are before this period and were not checked. Whether the Canada Cultural Spaces application was decided is not in the record.

title: Roads and a fire truck financed with 5-year local improvement debt
summary: Besides the water project, council financed several projects with short local improvement borrowing levied on all taxpayers and repaid over 5 years: Barkman Avenue underground renewal (2.33%), a new $800,000 fire rescue truck (100% debt), McKenzie Avenue reconstruction ($810K, up to $500K debt; only $300K borrowed after the work came in under budget) and the last phase of Elmdale Street ($1.05M surface works, $700K debt). All passed without opposition.
status_detail: Barkman debt By-law 2074 third reading Mar 7, 2017; rescue truck By-law 2089 and McKenzie By-law 2090 third reading Feb 20, 2018 (R18-034, R18-035); McKenzie debt issue By-law 2113 first and second reading Dec 18, 2018 (R18-295/296), third Feb 5, 2019; Elmdale By-law 2112 first and second reading Dec 18, 2018 (R18-285/286), third Feb 19, 2019.
figures: Barkman Ave debt at 2.33% over 5 years (Zwaagstra, 2017-03-07 0:13:40); rescue truck about $800,000, 100% debt (Warkentin, 2017-12-19 0:07:07); McKenzie $810,000 with up to $500,000 debt plus capital development reserve and a benefiting owner (0:09:49); McKenzie actual borrowing $300,000 at 3.29% for 5 years from TD Bank (2018-12-18 0:24:11); Elmdale surface works $1.05M with $700,000 debt (2018-12-18 0:10:50); 2018 plan: $6.7M new debt in total, all on 5-year terms.
reasons: pay-as-you-go: 5-year terms keep interest low. (Brian Hrehirchuk); infrastructure-first: Long-standing emphasis on renewing streets: 'expensive, but it's important to do'. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No objections were raised at the local improvement hearings for the rescue truck, McKenzie Avenue or Elmdale Street.
mover: Cari Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra / Damian Penner; Damian Penner / Jac Siemens
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Jac Siemens / Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra / Bill Hiebert
notes: The 2017 Barkman by-law's amount was not stated in the transcript.

title: 2016 surplus moved into reserves for capital development, land and the pool
summary: Unexpected revenue and cost savings left a 2016 surplus. On staff's recommendation council moved it into reserves for committed future spending: about $440K to the capital development reserve, $550K to the land and building reserve (land already committed) and $100K to the pool reserve, along with the routine yearly transfers.
status_detail: Approved Mar 7, 2017 (voice vote, no dissent heard).
figures: $440K capital development reserve, $550K land and building reserve, $100K pool reserve from the 2016 surplus (Warkentin, 2017-03-07 0:08:36); recreation reserve levy $1.1M in 2016, about the same budgeted for 2017 (0:21:54).
reasons: dont-burden-future: Putting money away is 'for the viability, long-term viability of the city'. (Chris Goertzen)
notes: No minutes for 2017; the mover is heard only as 'Councilor Penner'.

title: Provincial and federal money: cost-shared roads, gas tax and per capita grants
summary: Other governments paid a growing share of city projects: the province covered 50% of Main Street intersection repairs and all of the added work at the PTH 12 / Acres Drive intersection, leaving the city one-third of that $3.6M project; the city applied each year for municipal road program money; and the federal gas tax grant rose. In November 2017 the city was told the gas tax agreement requires asset management plans, with progress reported by Dec 15, 2017.
status_detail: Cost-share agreements approved without dissent; extra PTH 12/Acres spending of $571,150.40 (100% provincial) authorized Dec 19, 2017; asset management progress report to be filed by Dec 15, 2017.
figures: PTH 12/Acres Drive: total just over $3.6M, city share about $1.25M (one-third instead of half) (Zwaagstra, 2017-12-19 0:06:03); extra provincial-funded spending $571,150.40 (0:04:37); 2017 road program request $245,000 (2017-06-06 0:03:36); gas tax $730K (2017) and $765K (2018); per capita grant $2.36M (2017) and about $2.7M (2018, now including other grants) (hearings).
reasons: partner-money: Partnerships with the province are 'an important piece of how we can get things done in this city'. (Chris Goertzen)

title: Council pay raised after a citizen task force found Steinbach's council underpaid
summary: A three-member citizen task force chaired by L.M. compared Steinbach's pay with about 100 municipalities and recommended pay pegged to an MLA's $93,000 salary: $44,000 for the mayor, $18,135 for a councillor, $2,400 more for the deputy mayor and a $100-a-month technology allowance, with future changes following MLA pay. Council turned the recommendations into By-law 2084, effective July 1, 2017, and passed all three readings in June.
status_detail: By-law 2084 got first reading June 6, 2017 (dates amended to July 1, 2017) and second and third reading June 20, 2017. The roughly $20,000 cost for the rest of 2017 was not in the budget; the mayor said savings would be sought at the study session. By-law 2084 was repealed and replaced by By-law 2110 in December 2018.
figures: Task force: mayor $44,000/yr (half-time share of an $80,000 full-time figure); councillor $18,135 (30% of $60,450, itself 65% of the $93,000 MLA salary); deputy mayor +$2,400/yr; $100/month technology allowance; per diems indexed; future changes tied to MLA pay (L.M., 2017-04-18 0:18:05). Cost for July–December 2017 about $20,000 (2017-06-20 0:56:40, 0:57:22).
reasons: attract-candidates: Fair pay encourages 'quality members of our society' to run, and respects the task force's work. (Earl Funk); fairness-precedent: Questioned a clause indexing pay to staff raises when the task force tied pay to (frozen) MLA salaries; withdrew after clarification. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The task force (citizens; chair L.M.) concluded the mayor and council had been paid less than in most comparable municipalities and that the job is part-time and should carry no pension or health benefits.
vote: carried at each reading; no opposition heard
notes: Whether By-law 2084 kept every task force recommendation (e.g., the $100 technology allowance) was not checked against the by-law text. Seconder heard only as 'Councilor Penner'.

title: Audited statements and PSAB budgets accepted; auditor reappointed for one year
summary: Each year council accepted the audited consolidated financial statements (reviewed with the auditor Chambers Fraser) and a PSAB-format version of the budget showing the city's assets. Councillor Zwaagstra said the 2016 statements showed the city in 'a solid and healthy financial position'. In 2018 the auditor was reappointed for one year only, because of changes at the firm.
status_detail: 2016 statements and 2017 PSAB budget accepted June 6, 2017; 2018 PSAB budget June 19, 2018 (R18-145); federal gas tax expenditure report May 1, 2018 (R18-102); auditor reappointed for 2018 on Sept 4, 2018 (R18-202). All unanimous.
notes: The audited statements themselves (surplus, reserve balances, debt) were not reviewed for this file.

title: 2018 reassessment: smallest shift the provincial assessor had seen
summary: The provincial assessment office presented the 2018 reassessment (values as of April 1, 2016). The assessment base rose only about 1.1%, so keeping the mill rate the same would bring in about 1.1% more and leave the average single-family home with little change. Councillor Zwaagstra noted that in past reassessments a frozen mill rate still meant big increases for most people.
status_detail: Received as information before the July 2017 study session. In the 2018 plan, residential assessments fell about 1% on average, so the average city tax stayed at just over $100 a month despite the 0.16 mill increase.
figures: Assessment base +1.1% (assessor, 2017-06-20 0:47:23); 926 sales in Steinbach between Apr 2014 and Apr 2016 used (0:33:11); 2018 plan: residential values down about 1%, average dwelling just under $198,000 (2018-03-20 hearing 0:00:58).
notes: The assessor is a provincial official, shown by initials.

title: Supplementary water supply: $11M project, about half borrowed over 5 years, scope trimmed when bids came in high
themes: debt; capital-plan; utility-rates; provincial-funding; reserves; local-improvement
summary: The city's largest project to date, a new water supply and treatment system, was financed as Local Improvement Plan 2017-01 (By-law 2085) with $5.375M of debt and the rest from federal and provincial grants. When the low bid exceeded available funding in February 2018, council cut $754K of scope and used $230K of utility reserve and $414K of the 2017 utility surplus rather than raise taxes. The debt issue by-law (By-law 2114) followed in December 2018.
status_detail: By-law 2085 given first and second reading July 4, 2017 and third reading Sept 19, 2017 after Municipal Board approval; tender awarded Feb 20, 2018 (R18-032, unanimous) for a reduced scope; debt issue By-law 2114 got first and second reading Dec 18, 2018 (R18-297/298) and third reading Feb 5, 2019 (R19-030).
figures: About $11M total; $5.375M debt; 1.41 mills if the project were taken in isolation (2017-07-04 0:09:26, 0:14:09); low bid $11,342,984.22, deletions $753,791.63, $230K utility reserve redirected, $414K of 2017 utility surplus, award $10,589,192.59 (2018-02-20 0:08:47; minutes R18-032); $5.6M from other governments (Goertzen, 2018-02-20 0:11:25); debt at 3.29% for 5 years from TD Bank, lowest of 4 bids (2018-12-18 0:26:18).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Basic infrastructure needed for growth; the borrowing need not raise taxes if the budget compensates. (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: Unprecedented $5.6M from other governments; walking away would be an error. (Chris Goertzen); efficiency: Frugal years left utility surplus to cover the overrun without 'additional pain' for taxpayers. (John Fehr); pay-as-you-go: Debt repaid over 5 years per standard policy, which weighs on the next few budgets. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Two objections were filed to the local improvement plan (one written, one verbal); their content is not in the transcript beyond a concern about taxes. Resident T.M. asked why the city would borrow when, he understood, $5M sat in a reserve freed by the arts centre deadline; council said no such reserve existed (the recreation reserve held about $750K).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (By-law 2085 first reading); John Fehr (R18-032); Michael Zwaagstra (R18-297)
seconder: Jac Siemens; Cari Penner; Jake Hiebert
vote: unanimous at each step (none opposed heard or recorded)
notes: The face amount of By-law 2114 is not stated in the transcript (described as 'the full amount of the authorized borrowing'); $5.375M is the amount in the 2017 local improvement plan.

title: City buys 40 acres from the Fly-In Golf Club for $500,000 and leases it back for $1 a year
summary: After council turned down a $500,000 grant request from the Steinbach Fly-In Golf Club, the club offered to sell the city 40 acres of the course for $500,000. Council approved the purchase, paid over three years (about $167K a year) from the land acquisition budget, and a lease back to the club for about 63 years at $1 a year. Supporters called it a strategic land investment; opponents called it a bailout negotiated in closed meetings that undermined the grants process.
status_detail: Purchase and lease both carried on Dec 5, 2017. The first payment (about $167K) went into the 2018 budget, where opponents said it caused the 2018 mill rate increase; the 2018 plan passed 4-3.
figures: $500,000 for 40 acres, possession Mar 1, 2018; lease to about 2083 at $1/yr (Warkentin, 0:58:52); paid over 3 years, about $167K/yr, from a $300K/yr land acquisition budget (Fehr, 1:01:04); first proposed as 5 payments of $100K (Zwaagstra, 1:07:55); the club pays $25K+ a year in property tax (Siemens, 1:03:07). Supporters said the land is worth up to $1M; opponents said no appraisal was done (claims conflict; not verified).
reasons: land-investment: Land below market value, next to 40 acres the city already owns; within the existing land budget so 'no extra money'. (John Fehr); fairness-precedent: Grossly unfair to non-profits that are turned down for grants; creates a route around the grants process. (Susan Penner); transparency: Repackaged grant request, negotiated in closed meetings; 3-year payment schedule chosen to avoid Municipal Board scrutiny (his allegation). (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: A bailout benefiting the club and its lender; the city controls land use through zoning without owning it; no appraisal. (Earl Funk)
public: No public input was taken before the vote. Zwaagstra and Funk said a closed-meeting motion to have the club present at a public meeting was defeated 4-3 (their account; closed-meeting votes are not public). A Councillor Penner said the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce had written in support of the club. At the 2018 budget hearing Susan Penner said residents had overwhelmingly told her they opposed the deal.
vote: carried; by stated positions 4-3 (against: Zwaagstra, Funk and a Councillor Penner, almost certainly Susan Penner)
notes: No 2017 minutes; the vote was by voice. Which Councillor Penner spoke on each side is inferred, not stated. Whether an appraisal was done is disputed in the debate (a supporter refers to an appraisal 'much higher than our offer'; opponents say none was done).

title: Pat Porter Active Living Centre asks for a yearly grant in lieu of property taxes
summary: The seniors' centre told council it had run deficits totalling $38,572 over three years while paying $33,600 in property tax, and asked for a yearly grant in lieu of taxes and for council to rescind its policy of granting only to select organizations. The 2018 plan included no change to grants; the mayor said the policy is reviewed yearly and promised the centre would be told.
status_detail: Not in the 2018 financial plan (grants unchanged from 2017). The mayor asked administration to notify all grant requesters (minutes, Mar 20 hearing). No later 2018 decision found.
figures: Three-year deficits $38,572; property tax for the same years $33,600; 270 members, 4,500 volunteer hours, about 11,000 program attendances; Southern Health covers 24% of operating costs (delegation, 2018-02-20 0:17:04–0:26:01).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Council has a 'longstanding', 'simplified and focused' grants policy, which had not changed. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Delegation D.E. (president) and a co-presenter called the policy 'favoritism in the guise of fiscal management'. L.M. followed up at the Mar 20 budget hearing. Councillors Funk and Susan Penner contrasted the centre's treatment with the golf course deal.
notes: Also recorded in the advocacy data (2018-pat-porter-grant-in-lieu).

title: Water and sewer rates rise about $1 a month a year for 2018–2020 (PUB-approved)
summary: The city reviews water and wastewater rates every three to four years. Its May 2016 application was approved by the Public Utilities Board, and council gave By-law 2064 second and third reading: about $1 a month more for the average household in each of 2018, 2019 and 2020 (the 2018 plan described water steady and sewer up 11%). Rates had not changed since Jan 1, 2016.
status_detail: Second and third reading Mar 6, 2018 (R18-050, R18-051), unanimous.
figures: Average residential impact about $1/month in each of 2018–2020; rates unchanged since Jan 1, 2016 (Warkentin, 2018-03-06 1:00:07); sewer +11%, water unchanged in 2018 (Hrehirchuk, 2018-03-20 hearing 0:00:58); increases 'in the 3% range' (Zwaagstra, 1:02:13).
reasons: user-pay: Charge what the service actually costs; PUB has checked the rates. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: The first reading of By-law 2064 (likely 2016) is outside this period. Mayor Goertzen was absent; the deputy mayor chaired.

title: 2018 financial plan: mill rate up 0.16 (1.1%) to 14.09; passed 4-3 over the golf course payment
themes: budget; mill-rate; reassessment; policing-cost; debt; capital-plan; school-tax; utility-rates; fees
summary: The 2018 plan set the municipal mill rate at 14.09, up 0.16 mill (about $150,000), which the mover said covered the last three months of the higher RCMP share plus a pathway to Park Hill. Because 2018 was a reassessment year with residential values down about 1%, the average home's city tax rose under $3 and its total tax bill fell. Councillors Funk, Zwaagstra and Susan Penner voted against, saying the increase matched the first golf course payment (about $167K) and the deal had undermined the grants process; the plan passed 4-3, and the tax levy by-law passed on similar split votes.
status_detail: Adopted 4-3 on Mar 20, 2018 (R18-056). Tax levy By-law 2095 passed first reading 5-2 and second reading 4-3 on Apr 17 and third reading 5-2 on May 1 (R18-081/082/096). Business tax By-law 2096 kept the rate at 0.5% (unanimous). PSAB-format budget adopted June 19, 2018 (R18-145).
figures: Mill rate 14.09, up 0.16 (about 1.1%; about $150,000 citywide) (Hrehirchuk, 0:00:58 and 0:14:47); provincial education 9.77 mills and Hanover SD 15.143 mills (Warkentin, 2018-04-17 0:11:27); revenues just under $29M; property tax $14.9M ($14.1M by mill rate), about 51% of revenue; assessment growth about 3.3% including annexed land; average dwelling just under $198,000; average home: city tax up under $3/yr, total bill down just over $23/yr; supplementary taxes $525K; per capita grant about $2.7M; gas tax $765K; user fees just over $5M; 140 dwelling permits, $256K permit fees, $750K capital development fees; capital program $17.2M; new debt $6.7M, $2.4M repaid, year-end debt about $9M ($9.2M per Siemens), average interest just over 2.5%, debt payments $2.6M = 2 mills (just over 14% of the rate); sewer rate +11% (PUB), water steady, garbage just over +3%; labour $8.4M; protective services $4.1M with 16 RCMP officers (all 2018-03-20 hearing 0:00:58 unless noted); golf course payment about $160–170K (0:15:07).
reasons: policing-cost: Council had agreed two years earlier that new RCMP costs (about $800K) would be covered by new tax dollars; about $200K remained. (Jac Siemens); efficiency: Debt payments lower, debt management well within guidelines, reserves healthy. (Cari Penner); ability-to-pay: 'Not everything can be in each budget': no extra grants for seniors or youth, more pathways or a new recreation or arts facility this year. (Jac Siemens); fairness-precedent: Voted against: the increase matched the golf course 'bailout' and seniors following the proper grants process got nothing. (Earl Funk); transparency: Voted against: RCMP explanation 'recycled' from 2017; growth revenue would have balanced the budget without the golf payment. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Voted against: the golf deal compromised the integrity of the grants process; residents opposed it. (Susan Penner)
public: L.M., for the Pat Porter Active Living Centre, asked whether the centre's request for a grant in lieu of taxes was in the plan; it was not (see 2018-pat-porter-grant-in-lieu). No other public speakers.
notes: The 2018 hearing diarization merges several councillors under the same speaker labels; attributions rely on the chair's naming and the minutes' recorded vote.

title: 2017 surplus: almost $2M of unbudgeted money put into reserves
summary: At year end 2017 staff recommended moving surplus money into reserves: $300K to the capital development reserve for road renewal, $250K to the equipment reserve, $300K to start a yearly pool refurbishing program, and $550K of utility surplus to the utility replacement reserve. The mayor said almost $2M of unbudgeted money, largely capital development fees, was going into reserves, including over $1M into the recreation reserve.
status_detail: Approved unanimously on Mar 20, 2018 (R18-064). A month earlier, $414K of the 2017 utility surplus and $230K of utility reserve were redirected to cover the water supply tender overrun.
figures: $300K capital development reserve, $250K equipment and machinery reserve, $300K pool reserve, $550K utility replacement reserve (Warkentin, 2018-03-20 0:29:58); 'almost $2 million of unbudgeted dollars' into reserves and over $1M into the recreation reserve (Goertzen, 0:34:03).
reasons: growth-pays: Capital development fees are not budgeted until received, so they show up as surplus and go to reserves for future growth costs. (Chris Goertzen)
notes: The full transfer list is an attachment to the minutes and was not reviewed line by line.

title: City matches a $65,000 Co-op grant to repair the city-owned Arts Centre building
summary: Susan Penner moved to match a $65,000 Clearview Co-op Community Spaces grant with $65,000 from the recreation and culture reserve to repair the aging, city-owned Steinbach Arts Centre. On June 19, 2018 the majority tabled it 4-3 for more detail and a policy discussion; after the Arts Council presented its plan, council approved the match unanimously on Sept 4, 2018.
status_detail: Tabled June 19, 2018 (R18-148, 4-3); approved Sept 4, 2018 (R18-205, unanimous), funded from the recreation and culture reserve.
figures: $65,000 Co-op grant, matched with $65,000 from the recreation and culture reserve (minutes R18-205); the Arts Council planned to raise $20,000 more privately plus about $25,000 in donated goods and services (2018-09-04 0:32:04).
reasons: partner-money: Exactly the private-public partnership council says it wants; the building cannot wait. (Susan Penner); study-first: Ad hoc; if grant policy is changing, rewrite the policy first because 'we're setting a precedent'. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Wanted a concrete plan rather than 'throw money at something'. (John Fehr)
public: The Steinbach Arts Council (vice-chair A.B.H.) presented its repair plan on Sept 4, 2018.
mover: Susan Penner (motion); John Fehr (tabling); Susan Penner (R18-205)
seconder: Cari Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Cari Penner
vote: tabled 4-3 (against tabling: S. Penner, C. Penner, Funk); then unanimous
notes: Whether the grants policy was later rewritten is not in the 2018 record.

title: Three downtown lots bought for $647,400 to assemble a block on Hanover Street
summary: Continuing a long-term strategy to assemble downtown land for future development, council bought 336 Hanover Street ($194,500), 332 Hanover Street ($172,900) and 380 Hanover Street ($280,000) in 2018. Councillor Fehr voted against each, saying residents did not support the downtown development once planned there and the city had spent more than its land budget.
status_detail: Approved July 3 (R18-152, 5-1), Aug 7 (R18-174, 5-1) and Oct 16, 2018 (R18-238, 6-1); possession of 380 Hanover on June 26, 2019. No plan for the block was adopted in 2018.
reasons: long-term-vision: Assemble a large block for high-density housing, commercial or hotel use; continuity across councils. (Cari Penner); ability-to-pay: No public support for the downtown development; more spent than budgeted over 3-plus years. (John Fehr)
mover: Earl Funk; Cari Penner; Cari Penner
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Susan Penner
notes: The July 3 and Aug 7 debates were not read in full. The land budget amount referred to by Fehr is not stated.

title: Laptops for council members defeated 2-5
summary: At the new council's first regular meeting, Councillor Jake Hiebert moved that the city fund a laptop for each council member who wants one, for note-taking, research and keeping confidential material secure. The majority said paper packages work, the job is part-time and it was not a priority for tax dollars; some suggested a small technology allowance instead.
status_detail: Defeated 2-5 (R18-266). No technology allowance or laptop policy followed in 2018.
reasons: ability-to-pay: City tax dollars; not a priority; nobody campaigned on it; part-time role, use personal devices. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: No council technology policy; wanted a report from administration first. (Jac Siemens); ability-to-pay: Part-time ('maybe quarter-time') job; at most a very small tech allowance. (Susan Penner); efficiency: Paper works well at meetings; AMM reports councils moving back to hard copy; open to a small allowance. (Earl Funk)
vote: defeated 2-5 (for: J. Hiebert, D. Penner; against: Siemens, S. Penner, B. Hiebert, Zwaagstra, Funk)
notes: The 2017 task force had recommended a $100/month technology allowance; whether By-law 2084 included it was not checked.

title: Curbside garbage levy renewed: $133 rising $4 a year to $145 by 2021; residents ask for pay-per-bag
summary: The three-year special service plan for residential garbage collection expired at the end of 2018. The new council renewed it (By-law 2111) with the flat fee on the tax bill rising $4 a year from $133 to $145 in 2021. At the Dec 4 hearing two residents objected that small households pay as much as large ones and suggested pay-per-bag or tags; council kept the flat fee.
status_detail: First reading Nov 20, 2018 (R18-264) and second reading Dec 4, 2018 (R18-269), both unanimous; third reading Feb 5, 2019 (R19-028). The pay-per-bag suggestion was not taken up. A separate service complaint from an annexed-area resident was referred to administration.
figures: $133/yr now; +$4 in each of 2019–2021 to $145 (Warkentin, 2018-12-04 0:05:25). Earlier plan: about +2% in 2017 and just over +3% in 2018 (financial plan hearings). Solid waste services cost about $2.4M in 2018, funded by user fees (2018-03-20 hearing).
reasons: shared-cost: The service goes to every household; the truck passes each house regardless of how much garbage it has. (Michael Zwaagstra); shared-cost: Driving the route costs the same whatever the volume; urban living means sharing costs. (Earl Funk)
public: M.G. and A.O. formally objected: single-person households pay the same as neighbours who put out several bags; M.G. suggested pricing by bag or tags 'like other jurisdictions'. E.P., an annexed-area resident, raised missing service and notice.

title: New council signals no mill-rate increase for 2019; interim budget and $2M operating line approved
summary: After the October 2018 election the new council held a budget study session. In December, councillors said the 2019 budget would have no mill-rate increase ('a zero net increase, again, not even adjusting for inflation'). As every year, council approved an interim operating budget and authority to borrow up to $2M from RBC for operating cash flow (the same routine items were approved in December 2017).
status_detail: Interim budget (R18-275) and RBC borrowing authority (R18-276) approved unanimously Dec 4, 2018. The 2019 financial plan itself was adopted in 2019, outside this period.
figures: Operating line up to $2,000,000 from RBC for 2019 (minutes R18-276).
reasons: ability-to-pay: Council 'very mindful of responsible spending'; zero net increase. (Susan Penner (probable))
notes: Mayor Funk's earlier statement about the mill rate, referred to by Siemens, is not in the Dec 4 transcript (it may have been made at the study session or elsewhere).

title: Council pay adjusted (about $28,000 a year) to offset the end of the federal tax-free allowance
summary: Federal changes ended the tax exemption on one-third of elected officials' pay from Jan 1, 2019. The new council passed By-law 2110 to raise gross pay so take-home pay stays about the same, repealing By-law 2084, and said the roughly $28,000 a year would be found within the existing budget with no mill-rate increase.
status_detail: First and second reading Dec 4, 2018 (R18-280, R18-281); third reading Dec 18, 2018 (R18-294); all unanimous.
figures: Take-home loss avoided about $200/month per councillor and $400 for the mayor; budget impact about $28,000/yr (Siemens, 2018-12-04 0:45:03).
reasons: keep-take-home-pay: Not a raise in take-home pay; the federal government shifted the burden; Niverville, Brandon, Morden, Saskatoon, Regina and Yorkton did the same. (Michael Zwaagstra); efficiency: No new dollars: cost absorbed in the current budget. (Jac Siemens)
mover: Jac Siemens; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Jac Siemens
notes: Zwaagstra's list of other municipalities was not independently verified.

title: Purchasing and Tendering By-law updated; bid to delay it for more study defeated 4-3
summary: By-Law 2108 lowered public-tender thresholds to meet the New West Partnership Trade Agreement and raised staff purchasing limits for inflation (City Manager $250,000 to $350,000). Jake Hiebert, supported by Jac Siemens and Bill Hiebert, moved to send it to a Strategic Priorities Committee meeting so new councillors could study it; Zwaagstra argued it increased accountability and the motion failed 3-4. Second and third readings then passed unanimously.
status_detail: Postponement defeated (R19-011, 3-4); second and third readings (R19-012, R19-013) and policy (R19-014) carried unanimously.
figures: Tender thresholds: $75,000 goods/services (was $100,000), $200,000 construction (was $250,000) (transcript 1:00:16); City Manager limit $350,000 from $250,000; department managers $15,000 from $10,000; designated managers $75,000 from $50,000 (transcript 0:54:46).
reasons: study-first: In-depth document, many new councillors, $350,000 spending without council approval; wanted committee discussion first. (Jake Hiebert); efficiency: Changes mainly lower tender thresholds (more accountability) and adjust limits for inflation; no need for another meeting. (Michael Zwaagstra)
vote: postponement defeated 3-4 (for: J. Hiebert, J. Siemens, B. Hiebert); readings unanimous

title: Supplementary taxes on new construction added each year
summary: Council added supplementary taxes on new construction and improvements to the roll each December and cancelled amounts for demolitions and adjustments; the totals track what the financial plans budget for.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner
seconder: Susan Penner; Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert
notes: Routine yearly items grouped. The 2019 total is well above the $545,000 budgeted; the 2020 total is near the $635,000 budgeted (amounts before cancellations).

title: Public swim fees raised for the first time since 2008 to cut the Aquatic Centre deficit
summary: On the recommendation of the Strategic Priorities Committee, council raised public swim fees effective April 1, 2019 and added a child fee for ages 3-7. Damian Penner said the Aquatic Centre was running a deficit over $800,000 a year and had fallen below the 66% cost-recovery target set by earlier councils.
status_detail: Approved unanimously (R19-022).
figures: New fees incl. GST: adult $7.50, youth $6.50, child $5.00, senior $7.00 (R19-022); deficit over $800,000/yr, cost recovery about 58% projected vs 66% target (transcript 0:11:31); about $80,000 more revenue expected (transcript 0:13:32, Mayor).
reasons: ability-to-pay: User-pay: those who use the pool should pay more, though every taxpayer still covers much of the deficit. (Susan Penner)

title: Curbside garbage special service levy renewed
summary: Council gave third reading to By-Law 2111, renewing the special service plan that funds residential curbside garbage collection, after Municipal Board approval. Garbage rates rose 3% in 2019 and just under 3% in 2020 under the financial plans.
status_detail: Third reading February 5, 2019 (R19-028), unanimous.
figures: Residential garbage rates +3% (2019 plan, transcript 2019-03-19 0:10:37) and just under 3% (2020 plan, transcript 2020-04-07 0:21:12); solid waste services cost $2.4M in 2019 and $2.5M in 2020, funded by user fees.
reasons: efficiency: Renewal of an existing levy to keep pace with operating costs, not a new levy. (Susan Penner)

title: $5.375M borrowing for the supplementary water supply, the largest loan in city history
summary: Council gave third reading to By-Law 2114 to borrow the full authorized $5.375 million for the supplementary water supply project over 5 years, alongside a $300,000 McKenzie Avenue debenture (By-Law 2113) that came in under the $500,000 approved. Councillors called it the largest project and loan in city history and noted it made 2019 a tight year for debt payments.
status_detail: By-Laws 2113 (R19-029) and 2114 (R19-030) given third reading unanimously February 5, 2019.
figures: Water supply $5.375M at 3.29% with TD Bank (transcript 0:24:57); McKenzie Avenue $300,000 over 5 years (transcript 0:23:08); 2019 debt payments $3M = 3 mills vs 2 mills in 2018 (2019-03-19 transcript 0:22:08).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Upgrade basic infrastructure before problems arise, even though it is a large debt. (Michael Zwaagstra); growth-pays: Planning ahead so development can continue to grow. (Susan Penner)

title: Annual grant summaries approved; one-time library technology grant added
summary: Council approved the 2018 grant summary ($1,559,883.21, including $500,000 to the Bethesda Foundation) in March 2019 and the 2019 summary ($932,853.54, including $250,000 to Bethesda) in March 2020. In March 2019 it also approved Damian Penner's motion for a one-time $7,527.20 technology grant to the Jake Epp Library, which Susan Penner said fit the grants policy for one-time capital needs.
status_detail: R19-073 and R20-064 (grant summaries) and R19-076 (library grant) carried unanimously.
figures: 2018 grants $1,559,883.21: Jake Epp Library $327,315; Chamber $120,263.21; Mennonite Heritage Village $50,000; Arts Council $152,705; Bethesda Foundation $500,000 (R19-073). 2019 grants $932,853.54: Library $342,983.74; Chamber $129,869.80; MHV $53,200; Arts Council $155,400; Bethesda $250,000 (R20-064). Library one-time grant $7,527.20 (R19-076).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Library grant approved as a one-time special need, with a caution that the library already receives an operating grant and an increase. (Earl Funk)
mover: Bill Hiebert (R19-073); Damian Penner (R19-076); Michael Zwaagstra (R20-064)
seconder: Susan Penner; Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert
notes: Susan Penner spoke of a "$900,000 grant to the Bethesda Foundation"; the grant summaries show $500,000 (2018) and $250,000 (2019), plus a $200,000 committed reserve transfer, so the total commitment is likely larger than one year's payment. Not verified against a grant agreement.

title: Year-end surpluses moved into reserves for capital, land, policing and the pool
summary: Each spring council approved the prior year's reserve transfers. For 2018 (approved March 2019) surplus went to the capital development reserve ($675,000), a committed reserve for the Bethesda Foundation grant ($200,000) and the land and building reserve ($500,000). For 2019 (approved May 2020) transfers included $463,000 of transportation levies to capital development, $250,000 for future policing costs and $250,000 to the pool reserve.
status_detail: Approved unanimously (R19-074 March 19, 2019; R20-094 May 5, 2020).
figures: 2018: $675,000 to capital development reserve, $200,000 committed for Bethesda, $500,000 land and building reserve; recreation reserve $1,168,761 from the tax levy (R19-074; transcript 2019-03-19 0:44:06). 2019: $463,000 transportation levies, $250,000 policing, $250,000 pool reserve (transcript 2020-05-05 0:19:53).
reasons: reserves-low: Surpluses go to reserves so large projects can be paid without new taxes or long debt; "responsible budgeting". (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Developer's request for a $10,000-per-lot demolition grant denied
summary: A developer (L.W., Royal LePage) asked for a $10,000-per-lot demolition grant after Municipal Board conditions made a project more costly. Council unanimously denied it, citing Steinbach's developer-pay policy, the precedent it would set and the lack of any by-law allowing grants to for-profit companies.
status_detail: Denied unanimously (R19-075).
figures: $10,000 per lot; about 6 lots, ~$60,000 (transcript 0:49:56, Zwaagstra).
reasons: growth-pays: Development in Steinbach is developer-paid; taxpayers should not cover cost increases. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Developer-pay policy since the 1980s; precedent; grant by-laws only allow non-profits. (Jac Siemens)
public: Request by letter from developer L.W. (initials only).

title: 2019 financial plan adopted with the mill rate frozen at 14.09
themes: budget; mill-rate; debt; utility-rates; fees; capital-plan; process
summary: The first budget of the Funk council held the municipal mill rate at 14.09 (unchanged from 2018) despite a one-year spike in debt payments from the new supplementary water supply loan. Sewer rates rose about 8.5% (already approved by the Public Utilities Board), residential garbage rates 3% and most permit fees 2.5%. No member of the public spoke at the hearing; council adopted the plan unanimously.
status_detail: Adopted March 19, 2019 (R19-063); tax levy by-laws 2121 (realty and education) and 2122 (business tax 0.5%) passed April 2 and April 16, 2019; PSAB-format budget approved June 18, 2019 (R19-135).
figures: Mill rate 14.09, 0% change (minutes 8.6; transcript 0:10:37); revenues/expenses just over $30M; property taxes just over $15M; capital program just under $12M; supplementary taxes $545,000 expected; provincial per-capita grant ~$2.7M; federal gas tax just over $850,000; labour just under $9M; protective services $4.2M (16 RCMP officers, 39 firefighters); new debt $1.5M (fire rescue truck, Elmdale surface), $2.7M repaid, year-end debt ~$7M, debt payments $3M (= 3 mills, ~21% of city tax rate), average interest just over 3% (all transcript 0:10:37, Brian Hrehirchuk). Hanover School Division levy $13,990,168; provincial Education Support Levy $3,147,628 (minutes 8.4-8.5). PSAB restatement showed net revenue $5.7M (transcript 2019-06-18 0:29:15).
reasons: ability-to-pay: Property taxes do not rise with income; council made "tough choices" to freeze them, contrasting the city with federal deficits. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Borrowing only for capital, always repaid over 5 years; contrasted with long-term debt from operating spending. (Michael Zwaagstra); dont-burden-future: Council chose not to use the one-year debt-payment spike as a reason to raise taxes because payments fall again in 2020. (Susan Penner); infrastructure-first: Record infrastructure spending and the largest project in city history (water supply) were funded while holding taxes. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: First budget after the 2018 annexation; costs and revenues still being learned, so council held the line. (Jac Siemens)
public: No residents spoke at the financial plan hearing (minutes 8.9-8.10; transcript).
notes: Speaker labels E and A are mixed in this file (diarization); attributions rely on the chair naming the speaker immediately before.

title: New auditor appointed; audited statements and PSAB budgets accepted without exceptions
summary: With the long-time auditor leaving, council appointed Reid and Associates for 2019-2021. It accepted the 2018 audited statements (May 2019) and the 2019 statements (May 2020; no exceptions noted), and each year approved the budget restated to Public Sector Accounting Board format, plus monthly financial statements.
status_detail: R19-082 (auditor), R19-110 to R19-114 (2018 reports), R19-135 and R20-130 (PSAB budgets); 2019 audited statements accepted May 19, 2020 (no minutes on file for that meeting).

title: Business tax kept at 0.5%; Susan Penner questions the matching Chamber of Commerce grant
summary: Council kept the business tax at 0.5% (By-law 2122). Staff explained the city gives the Chamber of Commerce an annual operating grant roughly equal to business tax revenue, a practice dating from when the rate was cut from 1% about 15 years earlier. Susan Penner said the grant could compromise the chamber's independence and asked for a review; the Mayor agreed it should be looked at.
status_detail: By-law 2122 passed (R19-089/R19-090 April 2; R19-100 April 16, 2019). The Chamber grant continued: the 2018 grant summary shows $120,263.21 and the 2019 summary $129,869.80 to the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce (R19-073, R20-064). No review of the arrangement was found in 2019-2020 minutes or transcripts.
figures: Business tax 0.5% (transcript 0:31:59); Chamber grant $120,263.21 in 2018 (R19-073) and $129,869.80 in 2019 (R20-064).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Supported continuing for now so as not to "shock anybody", but said council should ask why it does things. (Earl Funk)

title: 2019 tax levy by-laws: council stresses that bill increases come from school taxes
summary: Passing the 2019 realty and education tax levy by-law, councillors said they must collect education taxes they do not control. Susan Penner said the system makes city taxes look higher than they are; Damian Penner noted the Hanover School Division levy rose 2.6% and the provincial levy 2.2% while the city mill rate did not change.
status_detail: By-law 2121 given first and second reading April 2 (R19-087, R19-088) and third reading April 16, 2019 (R19-099); unanimous.
figures: Hanover School Division +2.6%, provincial Education Support Levy +2.2% (transcript 0:30:18, Damian Penner); school levy $13,990,168 and ESL $3,147,628 (2019-03-19 minutes 8.4-8.5).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: City is required to collect education taxes; over half the bill goes to the school division; "not a lot we can do about it". (Susan Penner)

title: Applications to the Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program for roads, pipes and the pool
summary: Council approved ICIP green-infrastructure applications for Kroeker Avenue, Brandt Street and Loewen Boulevard (Sept 3, 2019) and a recreation-stream application for the Aquatic Centre renovation (Oct 1, 2019), committing the city's share. Earlier provincial Building Sustainable Communities applications for an arena chiller and a pool study were turned down.
status_detail: No ICIP approvals for these projects were reported to council in 2019-2020. Kroeker Avenue went ahead in 2020 as a local improvement with $1.77M of city borrowing, and the Aquatic Centre renovation went ahead in 2020 from the recreation reserve. The province denied the 2019-20 Building Sustainable Communities application (minutes Oct 15, 2019).
figures: City shares: Kroeker $781,431 of $2.93M; Brandt $1,389,507 of $5.21M; Loewen $750,761 of $2.815M (R19-177 to R19-179); Aquatic Centre $729,424.50 of $2.735M (R19-197). BSC requests: $39,606 chiller, $25,722.37 pool study (R19-122, R19-123).
reasons: partner-money: Projects are in the long-term capital plan; grants would "very much help our budgeting". (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Outcome of the ICIP applications after 2020 not checked.

title: Provincial assessor previews the 2020 reassessment: same mill rate would raise 3.4% more
summary: The provincial assessor told council that 2020 assessments (2018 market values) would, at an unchanged mill rate, raise municipal revenue 3.4% before new construction, with a slight decrease for single-family homes and increases for farm, commercial and institutional property. Steinbach's commercial share of assessment (33.5%) was described as strong. Zwaagstra asked whether an unchanged mill rate would be a net increase; council used this in setting the 2020 rate.
status_detail: Council cut the 2020 mill rate 2.8% to 13.70 to offset the reassessment ("net zero"; see 2020-financial-plan).
figures: Net +3.4% municipal revenue at an unchanged mill rate (transcript 0:31:19); commercial/industrial 33.5% of assessment; farmland +19.8% (transcript 0:34:07, Mayor).
public: Presentation by the provincial assessor E.K. (Manitoba assessment branch; initials used as he is not city staff).

title: Clearspring Greens pathway: neighbourhood asked to pay most of a $625,000 path; cost share revised after objections
summary: Residents of the rural-residential Clearspring Greens area asked for a safe pathway (July 2019 delegation). Council proposed a $625,000 asphalt, lit and fenced pathway as a local improvement, with each of 146 lots paying $4,280.82 (or $1,044.05 a year for 5 years); the city bought a lot for about $120,000 (about an 80/20 split). After a packed, objecting public hearing on Jan 7, 2020, a Siemens/Jake Hiebert amendment to cut the scope (limestone, no lighting) failed 2-5 and first and second readings passed 5-2. On Jan 21 council moved the $208,000 lighting cost to the city's capital development reserve (about 45% city / 55% neighbourhood).
status_detail: Objections continued (78 by January 2021). On Jan 5, 2021 council cancelled By-Law 2132 and replaced it with a plan with no lighting and the asphalt path split 50/50, capped at $1,610 per lot (By-Law 2168, third reading April 20, 2021) — outside this period.
figures: $625,000 total; 146 lots; $4,280.82 up front or $1,044.05/yr for 5 years at a maximum advertised 7% (transcript 2020-01-07 0:09:47-0:11:07); cost breakdown $270,000 asphalt, $78,000 fencing, $208,000 lighting, $69,000 other; city lot ~$120,000 (transcript 1:26:09, Damian Penner); after Jan 21: ~$2,800 per home, ~$570/yr, ~45/55 (transcript 2020-01-21 0:07:01, 0:11:40). Comparable Maplewood/Georgetown and Southland sidewalks were 50/50 local improvements (transcript 1:47:33).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Not willing to raise what everyone else pays; a neighbourhood-requested connector mostly benefits that neighbourhood. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Gas tax and reserves are committed to citywide asphalt overlay; every dollar moved here is not spent on general improvements. (Michael Zwaagstra); growth-pays: Path serves one neighbourhood (rural-residential zoning built without sidewalks); city paid ~20% via the lot. (Damian Penner); budget-constraints: In July 2019 the 2019 budget had nothing for the area; council must work within budget restraints. (Earl Funk)
public: July 2019 delegation of Clearspring Greens residents (M.F., P.R.; about 140-150 people attended) asked council to "find the money" for a safe path; residents noted their high property taxes.
