At the Jan 7, 2020 hearing many residents (e.g. D.B., D.J., S.F., J.W.) objected to the cost, the lot purchase and the lighting; staff reported 32 objections by Jan 21.
vote: 5-2 (against: J. Siemens, J. Hiebert) on readings; amendment lost 2-5; R20-012 carried 6-1 (against: J. Siemens)
notes: Residents named only by initials. The 2021 replacement plan is outside this period and is noted only as follow-through.

title: Event centre MOU: $10M city capital plus up to 0.5 mills a year for operating costs
summary: Council unanimously signed a memorandum of understanding with Southeast Event Centre Inc. for a $42.5M downtown event centre: the city commits up to $10M in capital and up to the equivalent of 0.5 mills a year for core operating costs; SEC raises at least $15M privately; $17.5M must come from federal/provincial ICIP funding before the project proceeds. Council also applied for the ICIP funding. Members said the deal gave a large facility for a quarter of the cost and could be paid without borrowing beyond the city's 5-year limit.
status_detail: MOU approved (R19-193) and ICIP application submitted (R19-198). The 2020 financial plan listed the "start of the events centre" in capital and $24.8M of 2021 capital including its continuation, but Zwaagstra said in April 2020 that it depended on government and private funding; no funding decision was reported in 2020.
figures: $42.5M total: city $10M, federal/provincial $17.5M, private $15M (minutes 13.2; MOU clauses 6-10); operating support up to 0.5 mills, ~$500,000/yr ("1 mill is about $1 million", transcript 0:33:01, Zwaagstra).
reasons: partner-money: Project proceeds only with $15M private and $17.5M government money. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: City share can likely be paid without borrowing beyond 5 years. (Susan Penner (probable)); infrastructure-first: Downtown site already serviced and mostly city-owned, saving millions. (Damian Penner)
public: Presentation by Southeast Event Centre Inc. (G.L. and K.G. for the group).
notes: Speaker K at 0:48:14 is unidentified in the transcript; attribution to Susan Penner is a low-confidence inference. Speaker E at 0:40:53 is a Penner, most likely Damian.

title: Residential and non-residential capital development fee by-laws adopted
summary: Council passed By-Laws 2127 (residential) and 2128 (non-residential) setting capital development fees charged on new development, the city's main "growth pays for growth" tool. The meetings (Nov 5 and Nov 19, 2019) have no transcript, so the debate and fee amounts are not recorded here.
status_detail: First reading Nov 5 (R19-214, R19-215); second and third readings Nov 19, 2019 (R19-224 to R19-227); all unanimous.
figures: Fee amounts not in the minutes. Related: 2018 reserve transfers show $226,566.93 transportation, $160,943 general, $95,491 sidewalk and $19,800 infrastructure capital development fees, and $35,225 water and sewer impact fees (R19-074). The sidewalk fee for a single-family home was $1,610 by January 2021 (R21-012).
reasons: growth-pays: Fees on new lots fund growth-related capital. (council (minutes))
notes: No transcript for Nov 5 or Nov 19, 2019 (videos not transcribed); no agenda package available for fee schedules.

title: Interim operating budgets and a $2M operating line of credit each December
summary: As the Municipal Act requires, council adopted interim operating budgets for 2020 (Dec 3, 2019) and 2021 (Dec 1, 2020) and authorized borrowing up to $2M from RBC for operating expenses at prime minus 0.25%, used only if cash runs short before taxes come in.
status_detail: R19-240 and the borrowing resolution (Dec 3, 2019); R20-246 and R20-247 (Dec 1, 2020); unanimous.
figures: Interim 2020 budget incl. $1M fiscal services, $1M capital equipment, $800,000 protective services (R19-240); line of credit up to $2,000,000 at prime -0.25% (R19-240 follow-on; R20-247).
mover: Damian Penner (R19-240); Susan Penner (R20-246); Damian Penner (R20-247)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Bill Hiebert
notes: Routine yearly items grouped. Dec 3, 2019 meeting has no transcript.

title: Five-year debentures for the fire rescue truck, Elmdale Street and Kroeker Avenue
summary: Council continued borrowing only on 5-year terms: $800,000 for a fire rescue truck and $700,000 for Elmdale Street (By-Laws 2138, 2139, first readings Dec 17, 2019, third readings Mar 3, 2020) at 2.78%, and $1.77 million for the completed Kroeker Avenue renewal (By-Law 2167, Dec 15, 2020) at 1.53%, which the City Manager called the lowest rate he could recall the city paying.
status_detail: By-Laws 2138 and 2139 third reading March 3, 2020 (R20-056, R20-057); By-Law 2167 first and second reading December 15, 2020 (R20-257, R20-258), sent to the Municipal Board.
figures: Fire truck $800,000 and Elmdale $700,000 at 2.78% over 5 years (2020-03-03 transcript 0:59:49, 1:00:58); Kroeker $1.77M at 1.53% with RBC (2020-12-15 transcript 0:46:23). Elmdale local improvement plan approved Feb 19, 2019 (R19-040, $1,050,000).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: All borrowing on 5-year terms. (Troy Warkentin)

title: Kroeker Avenue rebuilt as a local improvement funded by 5-year borrowing
summary: Council approved Local Improvement Plan 2020-01 to rebuild three blocks of Kroeker Avenue (road, water and sewer), with Municipal Board approval to borrow up to $2.21M. The tender came in at $1.797M, below estimate, which councillors credited to tendering early. No objections were filed.
status_detail: First/second reading Dec 17, 2019 (R19-248, R19-249); third reading and tender award March 3, 2020 (R20-051, R20-052); completed in 2020 and financed with a $1.77M debenture (R20-257).
figures: Borrowing authority up to $2.21M (transcript 2020-03-03 0:54:37); tender $1,797,432 (R20-052); ICIP application had sought $781,431 city share of $2.93M (R19-177).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Underground and surface renewal of an old street is a priority. (Michael Zwaagstra); efficiency: Tendering early gets multiple bids and best value. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (1st); Damian Penner (3rd); Michael Zwaagstra (tender)
seconder: Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert

title: COVID-19 in 2020: deferrals planned, provincial grant advanced, $947,679 Safe Restart money set aside
summary: In March council let the Mayor postpone or cancel April meetings, including the budget hearing, on 72 hours' notice. The 2020 budget went ahead with staff saying expenses could be deferred. The province paid more of the 2020 municipal operating grant up front because of COVID-19, and in November the city received $947,678.60 from the federal-provincial Safe Restart program; the Mayor proposed putting it in a reserve and choosing a project later. Building permits recovered to $58.5M by mid-December (vs. $81M in 2019).
status_detail: Meeting-flexibility resolution passed (R20-065); Safe Restart letter received as information Nov 3, 2020. No list of deferred 2020 items or a council decision on how to spend the Safe Restart money was found in 2020 records.
figures: Safe Restart $947,678.60 (transcript 2020-11-03 1:26:28); September operating-grant payment just under $300,000, total almost $1.2M (transcript 2020-10-06 0:26:41, Mayor); building permits ~$58.5M by Dec 15, 2020 (transcript 2020-12-15 0:42:29) vs just over $81M in 2019 (2020-04-07 0:21:12).
reasons: study-first: Put Safe Restart money into a reserve, then agree on a project. (Earl Funk)
notes: Whether any 2020 budget items were actually deferred is not stated in the minutes or transcripts; Sep 15, 2020 meeting has no transcript.

title: 2020 financial plan adopted at the start of COVID-19: mill rate cut 2.8% to 13.70 for the reassessment
themes: budget; mill-rate; reassessment; debt; utility-rates; fees; capital-plan; provincial-funding
summary: Drafted before the pandemic and adopted April 7, 2020 at a hearing where no member of the public spoke, the plan cut the mill rate to 13.70 (-2.8%) to offset the 2020 reassessment so average city taxes stayed about the same. Wastewater rates rose 9.5% (PUB-approved), garbage just under 3%, most fees 2.5%. Staff warned some items might be delayed or deferred because of COVID-19; council said the budget must still balance. The capital plan included the start of the events centre and Kroeker Avenue; doubled federal gas tax went to asphalt overlay.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously (R20-074); tax levy by-laws 2150 and 2151 passed May 5 and May 19, 2020; PSAB budget June 16, 2020 (R20-130).
figures: Mill rate 13.70, -2.8% (transcript 0:21:12; minutes 15.6); combined residential mill rate 28.342, commercial 37.170 (minutes); revenues/expenses just under $31M; property taxes $15.5M (57% of municipal revenue); property value growth 5%; capital $13.1M; supplementary taxes $635,000; provincial per-capita grant ~$2.9M; gas tax just over $850,000; labour $9.3M; protective services $4.2M (16 RCMP, 44 firefighters); new debt $2.8M (Kroeker, Clearspring path), $2M repaid, year-end debt $7.8M, debt payments $2.2M (2.1 mills, 15.5% of city rate); 2021 capital $24.8M (transcript 0:21:12). School levy $14,205,870; ESL $3,044,372 (minutes 15.4-15.5).
reasons: ability-to-pay: Mill rate lowered so the reassessment did not raise average taxes ("net zero"). (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Kroeker Avenue and asphalt overlay continue; core services continue during the pandemic. (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: Events centre spending contingent on government and private funding. (Michael Zwaagstra); dont-burden-future: Debt falling: $2M repaid, $7.8M balance "fairly low for a city our size". (Earl Funk)
public: No one from the public attended with questions (minutes 15.9).
notes: Minutes 15.11 say the Mayor commented on "highlights of the 2019 budget" (an error for 2020). Label I is shared by the presenter and Councillor Siemens in this file; quotes from I at 0:21:12 and 0:32:36 are the presenter by content and the minutes.

title: Aquatic Centre renovation moved up a year during the COVID closure, paid from the recreation reserve
summary: With the pool closed since mid-March and limited to 50% capacity on reopening, council asked staff to tender the lighting, acoustic panel and painting renovation planned for 2021 and awarded it in June 2020, funded entirely from the recreation reserve, so the pool would not have to close in summer 2021.
status_detail: Tender awarded unanimously (R20-118); pool reopening projected September 14, 2020.
figures: Tender $1,283,415; total project budget $1,479,415 (R20-118; transcript 0:20:37); initial estimate ~$1.3M (transcript 0:22:19); ICIP application in 2019 had proposed $2.735M total (R19-197).
reasons: efficiency: Do repairs while capacity is limited anyway, avoiding a 2021 closure. (Michael Zwaagstra); reserves-low: Funded from the recreation reserve built in earlier budgets. (Troy Warkentin)

title: Request for a 17th RCMP officer for 2021
summary: Council asked the province for one more RCMP officer under the municipal policing agreement, effective 2021, its first such request since 2014. Zwaagstra said Steinbach has about 1,000 people per officer and far fewer officers per capita than comparable communities; staff put the cost at $160,000-$180,000 a year.
status_detail: Approved unanimously (R20-243); a $250,000 policing reserve transfer had been made for 2019 (R20-094).
figures: 16 officers; ~1,000 residents per officer (transcript 0:10:57); $160,000-$180,000/yr per officer (transcript 0:13:56, Warkentin).
reasons: growth-pays: Population growth, drugs and traffic enforcement justify more policing. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Acres Drive local improvement levy kept on a disability-services charity despite its objection
summary: Local Improvement Plan 2021-02 would build Acres Drive in the industrial park with $3.1M of borrowing, levied by frontage on the two abutting owners: the city's own Steinbach Community Development Corporation and Envision Community Living. Two Envision representatives, including its board president, objected that the road gives them no benefit and the levy would cut services. Zwaagstra said a 2007 development agreement committed the property to its share at a 50% corner-lot rate (about $102,876, ~$20,000/yr) and exempting it would set a precedent. First reading carried 5-1, Siemens against.
status_detail: First reading only in 2020 (R20-251). Second reading April 20, 2021; referred to the Municipal Board (hearing Sept 9, 2021) — outcome outside this period.
figures: $3.1M borrowing (transcript 0:06:32); Envision share stated as up to $250,000 by the delegation vs. $102,876 by Zwaagstra (transcript 0:24:45).
reasons: fairness-precedent: City has never carved a property out of a local improvement; 2007 agreement explicitly accepted the levy. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Picking and choosing would recur with every plan; property value benefits eventually. (Earl Funk)
public: Envision Community Living (organization) objected through J.D. (speaking for the organization) and J.D. (president of its volunteer board): no benefit, funding comes from the province, the levy would mean cutting staff hours and services; notice came during a pandemic code red; about 75 signatures supported their objection.

title: Brandt Street water and sewer renewal approved as a local improvement
summary: Council gave first and second reading to Local Improvement Plan 2021-01 to replace or reline about 1,000 m of water and sewer line on Brandt Street: about half borrowed over 5 years and recovered by a utility-district mill rate levy, the rest from utility reserves and operating funds. No objections.
status_detail: First and second reading Dec 15, 2020 (R20-252, R20-253); third reading March 16, 2021.
figures: $2.415M total, $1.25M debt (transcript 0:34:38); ICIP application in 2019 had a $5.21M project with $1,389,507 city share (R19-178).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Timing is key: waiting raises costs; new relining technology lowers cost. (Susan Penner)

title: Clearspring Greens pathway levy redesigned after 78 objections: capped at $1,610 a lot
summary: A 2020 local improvement for a pathway to Clearspring Greens drew 78 objections from 146 parcels (about $4,200, then $2,850 per lot). Councillor Susan Penner moved to cancel it and replace it with a plan without lights, splitting the asphalt path 50/50 with the city's half from the Capital Development Reserve and capping each lot at $1,610, the sidewalk development fee new lots pay. The new plan drew 6 remaining objections and was built in 2021; 60 owners prepaid, cutting borrowing to $136,850.
status_detail: Old plan cancelled Jan 5, 2021 (R21-011) and third reading denied Feb 16 (R21-031); new plan R21-012; By-law 2168 first/second reading Feb 16 (R21-032/033), third reading Apr 20, 2021 (R21-076). Debenture By-law 2195 for $136,850 at 2.42% over 5 years: R21-276/277 (Dec 21, 2021), R22-046 (Feb 15, 2022).
figures: 78 objections of 146 parcels; prior cost ~$4,200 then ~$2,850 per parcel (transcript Jan 5, 2021 0:34:03); project ~$650,000; borrowing authority $233,450; 50% to owners up to $1,610 per parcel or $392.66/yr for 5 years (minutes Feb 16, 2021 7.3); actual debt $136,850 at 2.42% (transcript Feb 15, 2022 0:36:18).
reasons: fairness-precedent: $1,610 equals the sidewalk capital development fee every new lot pays (Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Earl Funk); ability-to-pay: over half the owners objected to the higher cost (Susan Penner)
public: 78 formal objections to the 2020 plan. At the Feb 16, 2021 hearing, 8 letters (7 against, 1 for); resident T.B. questioned why the plan was back after last year's objections, then withdrew his objection on hearing the lower $1,610 cap.
mover: Susan Penner; Susan Penner; Susan Penner; Jac Siemens
seconder: Jac Siemens; Jac Siemens; Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert

title: Application for FCM asset-management grant ($50,000 + $20,000 city)
summary: Council applied to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities for $50,000 toward asset-management software and a road-condition assessment, committing $20,000 from the 2021 operating budget.
status_detail: Application approved (R21-020); no public report on the grant outcome or the resulting asset-management plan was found in 2021–22 meetings.

title: How the budget is made: July and fall study sessions, a November review, near-empty public hearings
summary: Councillors described a year-round process: priorities set at closed July and fall study sessions, a final review in November, and adoption in March–April after a public hearing. No resident spoke at the 2021 or 2022 hearings. Councillor Damian Penner urged would-be candidates to read old budgets; Councillor Jake Hiebert told viewers the new council would spend a day and a half setting spending priorities at the fall 2022 study session.
status_detail: Study sessions remained unrecorded and their decisions were not reported in council meetings; only the resulting plan was presented at the hearing.
reasons: efficiency: every dollar accounted for in a balanced budget (Damian Penner)
public: No members of the public attended the 2021 or 2022 financial plan hearings (minutes).

title: Five-year debentures for Kroeker Avenue and Brandt Street renewals; Brandt overrun covered from utility reserve
summary: Council issued five-year debt for road and underground renewals: Kroeker Avenue (2020 project) at 1.53%, and Brandt Street (2021), where half the $2.4M cost was borrowed. When Brandt tenders came in over budget, council deleted the sidewalk portion and added $300,000 from the utility reserve rather than defer the work.
status_detail: Kroeker By-law 2167 third reading Feb 16, 2021 (R21-039). Brandt LIP By-law 2160 third reading Mar 16, 2021 (R21-057); tender + $300,000 Apr 6, 2021 (R21-065); debenture By-law 2194 ($1.25M at 2.42%) Dec 21, 2021 (R21-274/275) and Feb 15, 2022 (R22-045).
figures: Kroeker: authorized $2.21M, actual debt lower, 1.53% (transcript Feb 16, 2021 0:32:13). Brandt: $2.4M, half borrowed (transcript Mar 16, 2021 0:30:23); project budget to $2.715M with $300,000 from utility reserve (transcript Apr 6, 2021 0:38:13); debenture $1.25M at 2.42% for 5 years (transcript Dec 21, 2021 0:29:19).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: 5-year terms pay projects off quickly and get low rates (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: 'not doing this project is not an option' (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Susan Penner; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra

title: City grants about $1.05M in 2021; new $65,000-a-year Chamber economic development grant
summary: Council approved a five-year commitment (2021–2025) to match private funding for a Chamber of Commerce economic development office up to $65,000 a year. The 2021 grants summary totalled $1,048,420 (2020: $937,186), led by the library, Bethesda Foundation, Chamber and Arts Council, and including STARS at $1 per capita. Council also agreed to issue tax receipts for golf-club irrigation donations and pass them on as a grant of up to $180,000 at no cost to the city.
status_detail: R21-049 (Mar 2, 2021); grants summary R22-066 (Mar 15, 2022) approved without discussion; golf club R22-079 (Apr 5, 2022).
figures: 2021 grants $1,048,420.13; 2020 $937,185.54; library $336,680; Bethesda Foundation $250,000; Chamber $192,670; STARS $15,829 (R22-066). Chamber EDO up to $65,000/yr 2021–25 (R21-049). Golf club up to $180,000 pass-through (R22-079). Business tax 0.5% (see business-tax action).
reasons: partner-money: public-private partnership; city matches private funding (Damian Penner)
public: Golf club board member D.B. stressed the club was not asking for city money, only tax receipts (Mar 15, 2022).
mover: Damian Penner; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Bill Hiebert
notes: Speaker D at 2021-03-02 0:29:29 (sits on the Community Development Corporation with the mayor) is not named; not quoted.

title: Outside funding requests sent to unrecorded budget study sessions or received as information
summary: Requests from community groups were routinely deferred to council's July or fall study sessions or 'received as information': the Steinbach and Area Animal Rescue ($20,000 core capital grant, Mar 2021; again Dec 2021 and $10,700 in Nov 2022), Pat Porter Active Living Centre (Oct 2021), STARS ($1.50 per capita for four years, Sep 2022), and in Nov 2022 the Jake Epp Library ($49,000), Steinbach Community Outreach's The Bridge ($65,000) and a property-tax exemption for Adult & Teen Challenge. The mayor explained that once the budget is set there is no room to move money.
status_detail: No public decision found for most requests. The Animal Rescue does not appear in the 2021 grants summary (R22-066). STARS continued at $1 per capita in 2021; the outcome of the $1.50 request is not reported in 2022 meetings.
figures: Animal Rescue $20,000 (minutes Mar 16, 2021) and $10,700 (minutes Nov 15, 2022); Library $49,000; The Bridge $65,000; STARS $1.50 per capita for 4 years (transcript Sep 20, 2022 0:13:29).
reasons: study-first: budget already balanced; requests wait for the next study session (Earl Funk)
public: Delegations: G.P. and M.N. for Steinbach and Area Animal Rescue (Mar 16, 2021); D.B. for STARS (Sep 20, 2022). Other requests came by letter from the organizations named.
notes: Study sessions are not recorded, so the reasons for funding or declining these requests are not public.

title: First tax sale in years to collect five-year-old arrears
summary: To avoid losing the right to collect taxes unpaid for five years on one property, council designated 2016 as the tax-sale year, passed a Tax Sale Manager By-law (2169) and appointed TAXervice Inc.; it repeated the designation (2017) for 2022.
status_detail: R21-059 (Mar 16, 2021); By-law 2169 R21-070, R21-071 (Apr 6), R21-079 (Apr 20); TAXervice R21-080; 2022 designation R22-023 and appointment R22-024 (Feb 1, 2022).
figures: One property in the 2021 process (transcript Mar 16, 2021 0:34:57).

title: 2021 financial plan adopted with the mill rate held at 13.7
summary: Finance staff presented a 2021 plan with the municipal rate unchanged at 13.7 mills, utility rates unchanged, garbage collection up just under 3% and most permit fees up 2.5%, a $19.6M capital program (event centre start, Brandt Street utility renewal, asphalt overlays) and about $32M in revenue. Council adopted it unanimously, praising a 'no tax increase' budget built on growth and the five-year debt practice.
status_detail: Adopted Apr 6, 2021 (R21-064). The 2021 Realty and Education Tax Levy By-law 2171 (13.7 mills) passed first reading May 4 and second/third readings May 18, 2021 (R21-093, R21-105, R21-106); the PSAB-format budget was approved Jun 15, 2021 (R21-133).
figures: Mill rate 13.7, unchanged from 2020; capital program $19.6M; revenue just under $32M; $15.9M from property tax; supplementary taxes ~$650,000; provincial per-capita grant $2.9M; federal gas tax just over $850,000; labour $9.5M (about a third of operating); protective services $4.2M (16 RCMP officers); new debt $4.6M, $2M repaid, year-end debt $9.3M at ~2.7% average; debt payments $2.2M ($178,000 interest) = 2 mills, just under 15% of the city rate; average home just over $207,000 = city tax just over $100/month; future capital $28.7M (2022), $32.7M, $16.7M, $11.3M (transcript 0:19:59). Combined residential mill rate 27.95; Hanover School Division levy $14,163,826 (minutes; minutes misprint the municipal rate as '3.70 mills').
reasons: ability-to-pay: keep the mill rate steady because people have limited budgets (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: only 5-year debt, so projects are paid off and not carried for 20 years (Michael Zwaagstra); growth-pays: above-average growth lets the city manage taxes (Jac Siemens); infrastructure-first: underground infrastructure renewal is always a priority (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No member of the public attended the financial plan public hearing (minutes 10.9).
notes: Speaker letters identified from chair cues and minutes (no speaker map before 2022).

title: Provincial and federal money: per-capita grant, gas tax, disaster assistance
summary: The 2021 plan counted on $2.9M from the provincial per-capita grant and just over $850,000 in federal gas tax. Quarterly municipal operating grant letters and the 2022 provincial budget letter were received as information without comment. In August 2022 council applied for Disaster Financial Assistance for spring flooding.
status_detail: DFA request R22-198 (Aug 16, 2022); outcome not reported in this period. No council debate on provincial grant levels was found in 2021–22.
figures: Per-capita grant $2.9M; gas tax just over $850,000 (transcript Apr 6, 2021 0:19:59).

title: Acres Drive extension: $3.1M borrowing authorized, then cancelled when development funds and frontage levies covered it
summary: A local improvement (By-law 2161) to extend Acres Drive for industrial lots authorized up to $3.1M of borrowing; one objection sent it to a Municipal Board hearing. The street was built in 2022 below estimate, and in December 2022 council cancelled the borrowing authority because Steinbach Community Development Corporation funds and frontage levies invoiced to landowners covered the cost.
status_detail: Second reading Apr 20, 2021 (R21-081); Municipal Board hearing Sep 9, 2021 (R21-192); third reading Feb 15, 2022 (R22-044); tender $1,645,544 Apr 5, 2022 (R22-078); By-law 2219 cancelling the $3.1M authority given first and second reading Dec 6, 2022 (transcript; no Dec 6 minutes in the archive).
figures: Borrowing authority up to $3.1M (transcript Feb 15, 2022 0:33:08; Dec 6, 2022 0:18:12); tender $1,645,544.40 (R22-078).
reasons: growth-pays: frontage levies on benefiting landowners and SCDC funds cover the project (Troy Warkentin (staff))
public: One objection was registered and heard by the Municipal Board (minutes, R22-044 preamble).
mover: Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra (transcript)
seconder: Damian Penner; Susan Penner; a Councillor Penner (transcript)
notes: No minutes for Dec 6, 2022 in the archive; mover/seconder of By-law 2219 readings taken from the transcript and not fully certain.

title: Business tax held at 0.5%
summary: Council kept the business tax at 0.5% in 2021 and 2022 (By-laws 2172 and 2208). Councillor Siemens noted it was once over 12% and that much of it goes to the Chamber of Commerce.

title: Event centre land and design paid from reserves: 310 Hanover St, Reimer Ave lots, $1.9M design contract
summary: Council bought 310 Hanover Street ($475,000) and five Reimer Avenue lots ($1.4M, for parking) for the event centre site, paying for the lots from the Recreation Reserve, and awarded the architecture and engineering contract to Verne Reimer Architecture ($1,898,430).
figures: $475,000 (R21-097); $1,898,430 incl. disbursements (R21-199); $1.4M from Recreation Reserve (transcript Apr 19, 2022 0:22:09; R22-103).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: Recreation Reserve built up in advance so land purchases need no borrowing (Michael Zwaagstra)
seconder: Damian Penner; Jac Siemens; Susan Penner

title: Year-end reserve transfers: surpluses and federal Safe Restart money banked for big projects
summary: Council's annual reserve-transfer resolutions moved 2020's federal Safe Restart grant (~$947,000) and ~$1M of surplus into the Capital Development and Land and Building reserves, $370,000 of utility surplus into the utility replacement reserve, and $1.2M into the Recreation Reserve for the event centre. Members described saving surpluses as the way the city limits borrowing.
figures: Safe Restart ~$947,000; surplus $625,000 + $400,000; utility surplus $370,000 (transcript May 18, 2021 0:17:22); $1.2M to Recreation Reserve (0:21:35).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: saving surpluses limits borrowing and maximizes what can be built (Earl Funk)

title: Audited statements: 2021 surplus $9.1M, debt down to $6.1M, reserves up to $34.1M
summary: Council accepted the 2020 and 2021 audited financial statements from Reid & Miller after meeting the auditors, and reappointed the firm for 2022. Staff summarized 2021: a $9.1M accounting surplus (mostly contributed infrastructure), debt down to $6.1M and reserves up $5.6M to $34.1M ahead of large projects.
status_detail: 2020 statements R21-123 (Jun 1, 2021); 2021 statements R22-144 (Jun 7, 2022); auditor reappointed R22-233 (Oct 4, 2022). Monthly statements accepted routinely.
figures: 2021: annual surplus $9.1M ($8.4M contributed infrastructure); debt $6.1M (down ~$600,000); reserves $34.1M (+$5.6M) (transcript Jun 7, 2022 0:21:33). Audit fee $51,500 (R22-233).
reasons: efficiency: city run very well; auditor raised no concerns (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Jac Siemens
notes: The 2021 year-end debt ($6.1M) is lower than the $9.3M the 2021 plan projected; planned borrowing was not all issued (Acres Drive debt, for example, was never created).

title: Loewen Blvd / PTH 12 intersection: $3.5M borrowed over five years, province pays most of the rest
summary: Local Improvement Plan 2022-02 (By-law 2187) financed the $8.275M rebuild of the Loewen Boulevard / PTH 12 North intersection with $3.5M of five-year debt, $4.545M in provincial and other funding and $230,000 from reserves. Council called it its top provincial ask and money well spent.
status_detail: Engineering to WSP ($414,302) Jul 20, 2021 (R21-150); hearing and first/second reading Dec 7, 2021 (R21-250/251); third reading Mar 15, 2022 (R22-067).
figures: $8.275M; $3.5M debt, ~$853,000/yr at a 7% maximum; grants/other $4.545M; reserves $230,000; about $67.50/yr on a $200,000 home (transcript Dec 7, 2021 0:19:21).
reasons: partner-money: city pays less than half; province covers surface works (Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra)
public: K.P., speaking for the family owning the corner property, raised design concerns (turn lanes, median access, land taking) but did not object to the borrowing.
mover: Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Damian Penner; Bill Hiebert; Susan Penner

title: Extra RCMP officer for traffic enforcement requested (about $200,000 a year)
summary: After complaints about street racing on Main Street, Councillor Zwaagstra moved to request an 18th municipal RCMP officer dedicated to traffic from Jan 1, 2022, and to ask the province for authority to use red-light cameras. Members acknowledged the cost (about $200,000 a year) would affect the budget but said safety came first.
status_detail: Carried unanimously (R21-195). The officer was funded in the 2022 budget and cited as the main reason for the 0.4-mill increase (see 2022-financial-plan); in July 2022 Zwaagstra said the officer had been added.
figures: About $200,000 a year (transcript 1:05:57, 1:10:15); city then had 17 officers (transcript 1:00:47).
public: Letters from residents B.U., S.M. and L.D. about street racing on Main Street were on the agenda; the mayor said many more emails and calls had come in.
notes: Siemens's cost remark (Speaker J, 1:05:57) is not quoted because the label is not confirmed by a cue immediately before.

title: Event centre local improvement: $7.5M borrowed over five years toward a $42.5M project
summary: Local Improvement Plan 2022-01 (By-law 2186) authorized $7.5M of five-year borrowing for the Southeast Event Centre, then estimated at $42.5M, with an ICIP federal-provincial grant of about $17.5M, $15M in private donations and $2.5M from the Recreation Reserve. Council members called the city's roughly one-quarter share an exceptional deal and stressed the five-year payoff.
status_detail: First reading Sep 21, 2021 (R21-204); public hearing and second reading Dec 7, 2021 (R21-249); Municipal Board approval; third reading Apr 19, 2022 (R22-100). Costs later rose sharply (see 2022-event-centre-tender).
figures: $42.5M estimate; $7.5M debt over 5 years, annual payment just under $1.83M at a 7% maximum rate; ICIP just under $17.5M; private $15M; Recreation Reserve $2.5M; 1.53 mills a year for 5 years, about $138/yr on a $200,000 home (transcript Dec 7, 2021 0:06:16). Debt-to-assessment 1.37% vs Municipal Board 7% limit (transcript Apr 19, 2022 0:14:25).
reasons: partner-money: a bigger multi-use facility is what attracted $15M private and $17.5M government money (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: repaying in 5 years leaves room for the next project (Susan Penner); dont-burden-future: paid off in 5 years, leaving flexibility for other projects (Damian Penner)
public: Seven written objections were filed for the Dec 7, 2021 hearing: five from residents (M.H. & I.H., E.B., B.M. & A.M., E.B., L.D. & C.D.) and two from Haven Group and Steinbach Housing (signed by their CEO). No one spoke at the hearing. Zwaagstra said some letters questioned the project's size (e.g. 2,500 seats).
mover: Susan Penner; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner
notes: Turn timestamp for the Apr 19, 2022 Susan Penner quote is 0:15:12 (the published 2022–26 page links 915 s).

title: Supplementary taxes on new construction already counted in the budget
summary: Each fall council adds supplementary taxes for new buildings and improvements to the roll. Councillor Zwaagstra stressed that the amount (net ~$650,000 in 2021) was already budgeted, so it was not 'extra money'; 2022's adds were about $972,000.
status_detail: R21-242/243 (Nov 16, 2021); 2022 adds and cancellations approved Dec 6, 2022 (transcript; no minutes in archive).
reasons: efficiency: budgeting process accurate; no windfall (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Interim budgets and the RBC operating line: $2M a year, raised to $8M for 2023 because of the event centre
summary: Each December council adopts an interim operating budget and authorizes a short-term operating line of credit with RBC (prime minus 0.25%). The line was $2M (Dec 2021); for 2023 it was raised to $8M in anticipation of event centre expenses.
figures: Line of credit $2,000,000 (R21-257) then $8,000,000 for 2023 (R22-293), at RBC prime minus 0.25%.
notes: The 2022-12-20 speaker map lists label C twice (Warkentin high, Zwaagstra medium); the quoted turn is the staff introduction.

title: $1.34M provincial affordable-housing grant passed to Steinbach Community Outreach
summary: The province (MHRC) gave the city about $1.3M for affordable housing. After reviewing applications, council chose Steinbach Community Outreach's 24-unit low-income project, granted it $1,337,500, secured it with a forgivable 20-year, interest-free second mortgage (By-law 2210), and reduced the parking requirement.
status_detail: Variance with grant condition R22-052 (Mar 1, 2022); grant R22-161 (Jul 5, 2022); By-law 2210 R22-163/164 (Jul 5) and R22-185 (Aug 2, 2022).
figures: $1,337,500 (transcript Jul 5, 2022 0:05:15); 24 units; rents $583/$801 including utilities (transcript Jul 5, 2022 0:06:23).
reasons: partner-money: funding comes from the province; best proposal chosen (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Steinbach Community Outreach's executive director and a board member presented (Mar 1, 2022).

title: 2022 financial plan: mill rate up 0.4 to 14.1 (2.9%), mainly for an extra RCMP officer
summary: The 2022 plan raised the municipal rate from 13.7 to 14.1 mills (+2.9%), held utility rates, raised residential garbage rates 1.4% and land-use/permit fees 2.5%, and carried $25.3M of new capital (event centre, Acres Drive, Loewen sewer, sidewalks) and a $13.9M renewal program. Council said the increase was small and mainly paid for the traffic RCMP officer added in 2021.
status_detail: Adopted Apr 5, 2022 (R22-076, unanimous). Tax Levy By-law 2207 (14.1 mills) passed May 3 and May 17, 2022 (R22-107, R22-124, R22-125); PSAB budget approved Jul 5, 2022 (R22-169). The Apr 5, 2022 video has no audio, so the hearing is known only from the minutes.
figures: 14.1 mills vs 13.7 in 2021 (+2.9%); new capital $25.3M; renewal capital $13.9M; garbage +1.4%; fees +2.5%; utility rates unchanged; combined residential 27.83 and commercial 36.543 mills; Hanover School Division levy $14,061,502; Education Support Levy $3,093,339 (minutes Apr 5, 2022, 6.3–6.7).
reasons: policing-cost: 0.4 mill increase mainly for the extra RCMP traffic officer (Michael Zwaagstra); already-low-taxes: increase called minimal; council continues to keep tax rates low (Council (minutes 6.11))
public: No one attended the public hearing with questions or concerns (minutes 6.10).
notes: Hearing remarks (minutes 6.11–6.12) are not attributed to named councillors in the minutes.

title: Provincial assessor previews the 2023 reassessment: values up 8.3% on average
summary: A Manitoba assessor told council the 2023 reassessment (delayed a year by COVID) raised values 8.3% on average (residential 9.2%, commercial/industrial 7%, farm 5%); with an unchanged levy about 1,500 properties would pay more and 4,800 less. He also noted the provincial education property tax credit cut from $700 to $525, offset by rebates. Councillor Zwaagstra focused on the municipal levy, saying council has no control over school taxes.
status_detail: Received as information. Council accepted the 2023 assessment roll as amended by the Board of Revision on Nov 15, 2022 (R22-267); the 2023 budget then lowered the rate to 13.7 mills in the reassessment year (2022–26 report).
figures: Average +8.3%; residential +9.2%; commercial/industrial +7%; farm +5%; ~1,500 increases vs ~4,800 decreases at unchanged budget; education tax credit $700 to $525 (transcript 0:13:28–0:31:35).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: school taxes are outside council's control (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Presentation by provincial assessor R.S. (Manitoba Municipal Assessment Services).
notes: The assessor is identified by initials as a person speaking for an organization.

title: School division's request for a cost-shared school RCMP officer: city agrees only if the division pays 100%
summary: Hanover School Division asked the city to add an RCMP officer for schools on a cost-shared formula that, by Councillor Zwaagstra's reading, left the city paying about two-thirds. Council agreed to act as the contracting conduit only if the division covers 100% of the cost under a long-term agreement.
status_detail: Carried unanimously (R22-170): request approved subject to the division paying the full cost; the city's cost share was refused. Siemens's notice-period amendment was left to administration by consensus.
figures: Division's proposed formula: officer salary x 70% x 50% (transcript 0:26:09).
reasons: requester-pays: the division's initiative, so it should pay 100%; city already added an officer (Michael Zwaagstra); ability-to-pay: a second added officer would significantly impact the budget (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Request came by letter from Hanover School Division (organization).

title: Recycling contract, carts, garbage truck and landfill cell paid partly from the Environmental Reserve
summary: When Eastman Recycling quit, council contracted Bristal Hauling (about $566,600 a year, prices fixed 3 years, slightly above the old ~$500,000) and bought 6,500 automated carts (~$515,000 CAD) from the Environmental Reserve. It also expanded the landfill's active cell ($1.8M, Environmental Reserve) and covered a garbage truck that came in over budget from the same reserve. Garbage collection rates rose 2.8% (2021) and 1.4% (2022).
figures: Recycling $566,566.86 first year (R22-212) vs ~$500,000 before (transcript 0:20:46); carts $393,390 USD ≈ $514,947 CAD (R22-213); landfill cell $1,809,945.52 (R22-194); garbage truck $339,000 + tax ≈ $362,730 vs $320,000 budget (transcript 0:30:40); garbage rates +2.8% (2021 minutes), +1.4% (2022 minutes).
reasons: efficiency: contracting out recycling is most cost-effective (Earl Funk)
mover: Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner
seconder: Bill Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Jake Hiebert; Jac Siemens

title: New water and sewer rates proposed: about 3–4% a year for 2023–2026
summary: The 2018 rate plan expired at the end of 2020 and rates stayed frozen through 2021–22 (both financial plans held utility rates). In September 2022 council gave first reading to By-law 2163 with increases of about $1 to $1.35 a month for a typical home each year 2023–2026, subject to Public Utilities Board review.
status_detail: First reading Sep 6, 2022 (R22-209). After PUB review, second and third readings Dec 19, 2023 (R23-260, R23-261), outside this period.
figures: +$1.00 to $1.35/month typical residential per year, 2023–26 (transcript 1:33:25); ~3–4% a year (transcript 1:34:46).
reasons: cost-recovery: PUB requires rates as close as possible to the actual cost of service (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Event centre tender: $61M guaranteed maximum price, $13.2M more from reserves and operating, up to $5M more debt
summary: Bids came in far above the 2019 estimate (lowest $75.3M). After $14.3M of scope and specification cuts and a one-phase build (demolishing Centennial Arena in 2023), council awarded Graham Construction a $61M guaranteed maximum price. To cover the gap it approved $11.4M from the Recreation and Land and Building reserves and anticipated surplus, $1.785M from the operating fund, and a contingency plan for up to $5M of new debt; the Southeast Events Group raised its pledge from $15M to $25.5M. Members acknowledged the city was going deeper into reserves than intended but stressed five-year repayment and no further mill-rate impact.
status_detail: R22-254 and R22-255 carried unanimously, the first regular meeting after the Oct 26, 2022 election. The contingency borrowing became LIP 2023-04 / By-law 2223 (first reading Feb 7, 2023; third reading Aug 15, 2023), outside this period; a further $8.5M change order followed in Dec 2023.
figures: Lowest bid $75,333,000 less $14,331,000 of reductions = $61M GMP; about $66M with land and other items; reserves $11.4M; operating $1.785M; contingency debt up to $5M (transcript 1:29:01, 1:33:31; R22-255). City share about 35% (~$21–23M), of which ~$7M was already in the Recreation Reserve (transcript 1:39:06, 1:46:17).
reasons: partner-money: private sector raised its pledge to $25.5M; more grants being sought (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: still on 5-year lending despite the size (Damian Penner); dont-burden-future: 'not the council that is now going to be blowing up the future of our city' (Damian Penner); reserves-low: going deeper into reserves than council or administration would like (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No public speakers on this item.
notes: 'No further impact on mill rate' is the councillor's statement at the time; the 2024 budget later raised the rate 5.1% (2022–26 report).

title: Wastewater capacity: Lift Station 2 built, force-main twinning designed with provincial help
summary: To open east-side subdivisions, council upgraded Lift Station 2 (~$2.25M, part of an ~$8M program per Jac Siemens) and the Loewen force main, then sought Manitoba Water Services Board funding for half the design of the Lift Station 1 to lagoon force-main twinning and hired engineers for it in Nov 2024. Michael Zwaagstra flagged lagoon expansion and eventual mechanical wastewater treatment as growth costs that development fees help fund.
status_detail: Lift Station 2 upgrade awarded Oct 17, 2023 (R23-213) and financed by $2M debt (2024); MWSB request Jun 18, 2024 (R24-127); engineering for lift station upgrades and force-main twinning awarded Nov 5, corrected to $463,201 Nov 19, 2024 (R24-209, R24-223). Larger treatment expansion not yet funded in this period.
figures: Lift Station 2: $2.265M plan, low bid $1,996,642.57 + $250,000 reserve; Loewen force main $491,693; engineering $463,201 (minutes). Overall program ~'$8 million' (J. Siemens, Oct 17, 2023 - medium-confidence speaker).
reasons: growth-pays: Lagoon expansion and mechanical treatment are growth costs development fees help fund. (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: Apply to MWSB so the city can access provincial funding. (Damian Penner)
seconder: J. Siemens; M. Zwaagstra; D. Penner
notes: The 2025-2026 wastewater expansion (city share $65M+) is outside this period.

title: Three borrowing by-laws for 2023 projects: ladder truck, Lift Station 2, Barkman Avenue
summary: Council held public hearings (no one objected) and passed local-improvement borrowing by-laws for a fire ladder truck ($2M), the Lift Station 2 upgrade ($2M of $2.265M; rest from the utility reserve) and Barkman Avenue/Penner Street renewal ($1.12M of $2.6M; rest from reserves), all repayable over 5 years with an 8% maximum rate. The ladder truck later cost $136,000 more than planned. A $3.1M borrowing authority for Acres Drive was cancelled because the work came in under estimate.
status_detail: First and second readings Jan 3, 2023; third readings Mar 21, 2023 after Municipal Board approval (R23-052, R23-054, R23-055). Ladder truck bought May 2, 2023 for $2,135,475.14 (R23-080). Acres Drive authority cancelled Feb 21, 2023 (R23-040). Lift Station 2 and Barkman debt actually issued in 2024 at 5.41% (see 2024-debenture-issues).
figures: Ladder truck up to $2M; Lift Station 2 $2.265M total, $2M borrowed (~$500,000/yr payment); Barkman/Penner $2.6M total, $1.12M borrowed; max interest 8% (was 7% in earlier by-laws) (transcript Jan 3, 2023 0:06:31-0:16:04); ladder truck $2,135,475.14, +$136,000 (minutes R23-080; transcript May 2, 2023 0:21:01); Acres Drive $3.1M authority cancelled (minutes R23-040).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Basic infrastructure remains the top priority; the money is well spent. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: 8% is only a ceiling so a new hearing isn't needed if rates rise; five-year repayment. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Staying ahead of renewal saves money in the long run. (Susan Penner)
public: No one attended or wrote in on any of the three hearings (transcript Jan 3, 2023; minutes).
mover: various (2220: D. Penner/J. Hiebert; 2221: J. Siemens/M. Zwaagstra; 2222: S. Penner/B. Hiebert at first reading)
notes: Acres Drive cancellation's first readings were Dec 6, 2022 (outside period); third reading Feb 21, 2023 has no recording, so it is from the minutes only.

title: Extra $5M borrowing authority approved as an Event Centre contingency
summary: As directed when the Event Centre tender was awarded (Nov 1, 2022), council passed By-law 2223 authorizing up to $5M more borrowing (5-year term, 8% maximum, later 7%) in case of unforeseen costs, so the project would not drain reserves further or hit the operating budget. No one objected at the hearing. Members said they hoped not to use it.
status_detail: First/second reading Feb 7, 2023; Municipal Board approved (Order E-23-01); third reading Aug 15, 2023 (R23-169). In Dec 2023 council drew $2.5M of it toward the $8.153M change order.
figures: Up to $5M, 5 years, max 8% (Feb 7) / 'no greater than 7%' (Aug 15) (transcript Feb 7, 2023 0:06:32; Aug 15, 2023 0:21:08); $2.5M used (R23-252).
reasons: reserves-low: Avoid going deeper into reserves or affecting the operating budget if costs rise. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Prudent, proactive; any loan repaid within 5 years per council policy. (Jake Hiebert); partner-money: Grant applications pending could make the borrowing unnecessary. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No one present at the hearing and no written objections (minutes Feb 7, 2023).

title: About $1-1.3M a year in grants to groups; new requests sent to unrecorded study sessions
summary: The 2022 grant summary showed $1.27M, led by the Jake Epp Library, the Bethesda Foundation, the Chamber and the Arts Council; budgets set grants at ~$1.3M (2023) and just over $1M (2024). New funding asks were not decided in public: Steinbach Minor Hockey's request (Oct 2023) went to the November study session, Southeast Cancer Support Services' $40,000 operating-grant request (Jun 2024) was taken back to administration, and many letters were 'received as information'. The city kept its $1-per-capita STARS donation.
status_detail: 2022 grant summary accepted Feb 21, 2023 (R23-039). No public decision on the minor hockey or Southeast Cancer Support Services requests was found in 2023-2024 meeting records.
figures: 2022 grants $1,267,189.95: Jake Epp Library $336,680; Bethesda Foundation $250,000; Chamber $208,542.20; Arts Council $166,317.26; Golf Club irrigation $132,700; Serving Seniors transit $102,921.49; MHV $52,500; STARS $15,829 (minutes R23-039). Grants ~$1.3M (2023 budget), just over $1M (2024 budget). Physician resident retreat up to $10,000 from 2023 surplus (R23-153). SE Cancer Support request $40,000 (minutes Jun 18, 2024).
reasons: study-first: Financial asks are fairer to decide at study session with the whole budget in front of council. (Earl Funk); fairness-precedent: Asked whether regional groups are also seeking money from neighbouring municipalities. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Southeast Cancer Support Services (H.J., C.R.P.) described transportation costs for cancer patients and asked for a $40,000 operating grant; STARS (D.B.) thanked the city for $1 per capita.
notes: Study-session outcomes are not recorded; the existing report also notes these requests went to unrecorded sessions.

title: Province raises operating and per-capita grants after years of freezes
summary: In 2023 the province sent an unconditional per-capita grant, increased the municipal operating grant, added $1.356M in per-capita strategic infrastructure money, raised the urban policing grant, and added $1M to its Event Centre grant. Council received the letters as information and welcomed the money as project costs climbed. The per-capita grant in the budget rose from $3M (2023) to $4.6M (2024).
status_detail: Received as information (Mar 7, Apr 4, Jun 20, Oct 17 and Aug 15, 2023; Jul 2, 2024). Extra money was used in the 2024 budget and the Event Centre funding package.
figures: Per-capita tax-sharing grant $3M budgeted 2023 vs $4.6M 2024; federal gas tax ~$890,000 both years (staff presentations Mar 21, 2023 0:12:14; Apr 2, 2024 0:08:30). Final 2023 operating grant payment $811,293.35 (transcript Oct 17, 2023 0:27:35). Strategic infrastructure per-capita $1.356M; provincial pool of $44M for 2024 projects; Event Centre +$1M (transcript Aug 15, 2023 0:29:27-0:30:05). Urban policing grant +28% (0:28:54).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Province recognized municipalities' rising construction costs. (Earl Funk)
notes: Exact grant letters were not reviewed; amounts are as stated at the meetings.

title: Council repeatedly reaffirms its rule of repaying all debt within 5 years
summary: Across both years members cited the long-standing practice of repaying every loan within five years as the reason Steinbach can afford the Event Centre and keep interest low, and said they did not want to deviate from it. It is a practice, not a written by-law; the 2024 debt load was the highest in years.
status_detail: Every debt issued in 2023-2024 (Lift Station 2, Barkman, PTH 12/Loewen, Event Centre) used a 5-year term. No written debt policy was adopted.
figures: 5-year amortization for all debt; avg interest ~2.4% (2023) and ~4.2% (2024); year-end debt projected ~$14M (2023) and ~$19.5M (2024); debt payments 1.8 mills (2023) and 1.27 mills (2024) (staff presentations). Audited long-term debt $1.9M (2023), $11.0M (2024) per existing report.
reasons: dont-burden-future: Five-year rule keeps future councils free to do new projects. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Shorter terms mean less interest. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: No member questioned the rule in 2023-2024; the wastewater challenge to it was raised in 2025 (outside this period).

title: 2023 financial plan: city mill rate cut 2.8% to 13.7 in a reassessment year
themes: budget; mill-rate; reassessment; debt; capital-plan; process
summary: Staff presented a 2023 plan with $34.5M in operating revenue, a $67.3M capital program led by the Event Centre, and a city mill rate of 13.7 (down 2.8% as assessments rose 10.8% in the reassessment year). No one from the public spoke at the hearing. Council adopted it unanimously; members described it as aggressive on infrastructure while 'mindful' of ability to pay, and said the plan was shaped over 'weekends' of study sessions.
status_detail: Financial plan adopted Mar 21, 2023 (R23-053); tax levy By-law 2225 given readings May 2 and May 16, 2023; a PSAB-adjusted version of the budget was adopted Jun 20, 2023 (R23-129) on the auditors' advice.
figures: Mill rate 13.7, -2.8% (transcript 0:08:50); property value growth 10.8%; revenue/expenses $34.5M; $18M from property tax; average home ~$217,000, city tax ~$111/month; supplementary taxes budgeted $550,000; provincial per-capita grant $3M; federal gas tax ~$890,000; grants to organizations ~$1.3M; labour $10.7M; protective services $4.6M incl. 18 RCMP officers and 49 firefighters; capital $67.3M; ~$12M new debt, $2.1M repaid; average interest ~2.4%; year-end debt ~$14M; debt payments $2.2M = 1.8 mills (~13% of city rate); utility rates +4% avg, garbage +2.7%; out-years $36.1M (2024), $22.7M, $26.5M, $19.5M (staff presentation 0:08:50-0:19:39, Mar 21, 2023).
reasons: ability-to-pay: Budget is a balancing act; council must be mindful of residents' ability to pay. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Budget reflects priorities of infrastructure renewal/expansion and recreation facility renewal. (Mayor Earl Funk); dont-burden-future: Five-year debt policy means future councils are not hamstrung; it is why the Event Centre is affordable. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Big numbers reflect what the city is responsible for: 140 km of roads, 200+ km of pipe, recreation. (Jac Siemens)
public: No one spoke or objected at the public hearing (transcript 0:19:52).
notes: 2023 budget figures are from the staff presentation at the hearing (transcript). The 2022 hearing is outside this period.

title: Policing: 18 RCMP officers kept; RCMP multi-year plan accepted
summary: Both budgets kept 18 RCMP officers; protective services rose from $4.6M (2023) to $5.1M (2024). Council accepted the RCMP's 2024-2029 multi-year financial plan, noting most costs (such as national salary increases) are outside the city's control. The provincial urban policing grant rose 28% in 2023. In the 2024 budget debate Jac Siemens cited the city's larger share of RCMP costs since passing 15,000 people.
status_detail: RCMP plan accepted Jul 4, 2023 (R23-140). Officer count held at 18 in 2023 and 2024 budgets.
figures: Protective services $4.6M (2023), $5.1M (2024) incl. 18 RCMP officers (staff presentations). Urban policing grant +28% (Mayor, Aug 15, 2023 0:28:54). Cost-share percentages stated by J. Siemens (25% / 95%) are as spoken and not verified.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: RCMP plan set nationally; city has little control over the costs. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Siemens' percentages differ from the usual RCMP contract cost-share (70% municipal under 15,000; 90% over); treat as spoken, unverified.

title: Tenders over budget: scope cut, work deferred and reserves tapped
summary: Construction inflation pushed several 2023 tenders over budget. Council dropped Penner Street from the Barkman Avenue job and deferred part of Lift Station 2 to cover a $690,000 overage, added $250,000 from the utility reserve when the Lift Station 2 bid came in near $2M against a ~$1.7M estimate, and cut scope on the 2024 Loewen force main. It also used reserves to pave Park Road West through to Industrial Road while a developer was building. By March 2024 one tender came in under estimate.
status_detail: All awards carried unanimously (R23-057, R23-058, R23-213, R24-064, R24-065). Projects went ahead, but with reduced scope (Penner Street portion removed; force main scope reduced).
figures: Barkman/Penner/overlay low bid $3,445,402 after removing Penner St (~$300,000 saved), $265,000 freed from Lift Station 2, $120,000 utility reserve; overage $690,000 (transcript Mar 21, 2023 0:53:49-0:57:01). Park Road West extension $1,970,097 (R23-057). Lift Station 2 low bid $1,996,642.57 vs estimate just under $1.7M; +$250,000 utility replacement reserve (transcript Oct 17, 2023 0:22:35-0:24:13; R23-213). Loewen force main sole bid $570,310 cut to $491,693 (Mar 19, 2024; R24-065). 2024 capital works $1,324,707, under estimate (R24-064).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Basic infrastructure must go ahead even when tenders come in high. (Michael Zwaagstra); reserves-low: Healthy reserves let the city piggyback on developer work. (Damian Penner)

title: Water and sewer rates set for 2024-2027 at about 3-4% a year
summary: After Public Utilities Board approval (Order 137-23), council gave final readings to By-law 2163, a four-year rate plan raising a typical home's water and sewer bill 3-4% a year on a cost-recovery basis. The 2023 and 2024 budgets also raised utility rates about 4% and garbage rates 2.7% and 2.6%.
status_detail: Second and third readings Dec 19, 2023 (R23-260, R23-261); first reading was earlier (before this period).
figures: Typical residential increase 3-4%/yr, 2024-2027 (transcript Dec 19, 2023 0:48:43); utility rates +4% avg in 2023 and 2024; garbage +2.7% (2023), +2.6% (2024) (staff presentations).
reasons: efficiency: Rates are set on a cost-recovery basis, reviewed by the PUB. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: PTH 12 / Loewen intersection: $9.98M contract, city share about $5.8M
summary: After years of postponement, council awarded the PTH 12 North/Loewen Boulevard renewal to the low bidder within the ~$10.4M budget. The province pays above-ground highway work (about $4-4.5M plus signals and utilities); the city pays underground utilities and its share (~$5.8M) from operating and utility funds, reserves and two 5-year debt issues.
status_detail: Tender awarded May 21, 2024 (R24-107); completion expected fall 2025.
figures: Contract $9,981,284; budget just under $10.4M, ~$4.5M from the province (City Manager, transcript May 21, 2024 0:19:35). City ~$5.8M: general operating ~$1M+, utility operating $80,000, utility reserve $1.1M, capital development reserve $110,000, general debt $1.4M, utility debt $2.1M (J. Siemens, 0:23:00).
reasons: partner-money: Done in partnership with the province; last major Highway 12 intersection. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Provincial share given as ~$4M (Siemens) and ~$4.5M (City Manager).

title: Business tax kept at 0.5%, passed through to the Chamber of Commerce
summary: Council renewed the 0.5% business tax each year; the city keeps a small administration fee and remits the rest to the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce as operating funding. Susan Penner noted the amount grows automatically with assessment. (In 2025 she and the mayor asked for it to be reviewed; outside this period.)
status_detail: By-law 2226 (2023) and By-law 2248 (2024) passed unanimously.
figures: Business tax rate 0.5%, unchanged (transcript May 2, 2023 0:38:10; Apr 16, 2024 0:48:47). Chamber received $208,542.20 in 2022 (2022 grant summary, R23-039).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Long-standing arrangement the business community appears to support. (Susan Penner)

title: Southeast Events Group's $25.5M private pledge secured in writing
summary: Council approved an 'assignment of proceeds from pledge agreements' with the Southeast Events Group Foundation, securing the group's private fundraising for the Event Centre as the 2019 MOU required.
status_detail: Approved May 2, 2023 (R23-081).
figures: $25.5M in private contributions (transcript May 2, 2023 0:25:44).
reasons: partner-money: Project would not be happening this way without the private partner. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Year-end surpluses moved to reserves, including $2.1M for the Event Centre
summary: Approving the 2022 reserve transfers, council put unbudgeted year-end revenue into reserves: $2.1M to the land and building reserve for Event Centre contingencies and $210,000 to the environmental reserve. Development fees brought in about $1.8-1.9M against $615,000 budgeted. Members said building reserves is what lets Steinbach take on large projects and borrow less. The 2023 transfers were ratified in June 2024 without debate.
status_detail: 2022 transfers approved May 16, 2023 (R23-102, Zwaagstra/D. Penner); 2023 transfers approved Jun 18, 2024 (R24-126, S. Penner/Zwaagstra).
figures: Land & building reserve +$2.1M; environmental reserve +$210,000; capital development fees ~$1.8-1.9M collected vs $615,000 budgeted (City Manager, transcript May 16, 2023 0:14:35). Reserve funds $38.7M at end of 2022 (transcript Jun 6, 2023 0:14:03); $44.3M end of 2023 and $38.6M end of 2024 (audited, per the existing 2022-2026 report).
reasons: reserves-low: Put surplus in reserves because of known future requirements and Event Centre contingencies. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Cash on hand reduces what must go on debenture. (Damian Penner); dont-burden-future: Past councils' foresight in saving made the Event Centre possible. (Earl Funk)
notes: The 2024 reserve balance is from the audited figures quoted in answers/taxes-spending/ (not re-checked here).

title: Audited statements for 2022 and 2023 accepted: surpluses, growing reserves
summary: Council accepted the 2022 audited statements (Jun 2023), which showed a $7.1M surplus ($3.3M of it contributed infrastructure from developers) and reserves up to $38.7M, and the 2023 statements (Jun 2024), where staff reported no unusual items. Council meets the auditor in an unrecorded session before acceptance; members said the audits confirm a strong position. Reid & Miller was reappointed each year.
status_detail: 2022 audit accepted Jun 6, 2023 (R23-112, Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert); 2023 audit accepted Jun 18, 2024 (R24-125, Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert). Auditor reappointed Oct 17, 2023 ($57,500, R23-214) and Aug 20, 2024 ($60,500, R24-167).
figures: 2022 surplus $7.1M incl. $3.3M contributed infrastructure; $12M+ tangible capital assets added; reserves $38.7M at end of 2022 (transcript Jun 6, 2023 0:12:56-0:14:03). Audit fee $57,500 (2023), $60,500 (2024) (minutes). Long-term debt $1.9M end of 2023 and $11.0M end of 2024; reserves $44.3M end of 2023 (audited, per existing report).
reasons: efficiency: Audit confirms year after year the city is in a solid financial position. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Audit meetings with council are not recorded.

title: Council backs AMM resolutions against provincial cost downloading and grant strings
summary: Council sponsored two AMM district resolutions: one asking the province to end 'lift-assist' calls that send paid-on-call firefighters to do EMS work, and Winkler's call to drop the 10% non-government funding rule in the Building Sustainable Communities program. A resolution on fair allocation of policing costs was received as information.
status_detail: Both sponsored Jun 6, 2023 (R23-118, R23-119). No provincial response reported at council in this period.
figures: Fire department ~300 calls a year; lift assists rising from 1-3 a year to a projected 40-60 (Mayor, transcript Jun 6, 2023 0:41:11, 0:44:46).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Health care is provincial; downloading strains municipal fire services. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Small municipalities lack Steinbach's private donors to meet the 10% rule. (Damian Penner)
vote: unanimous (R23-119 vote not captured by parser)

title: Asset management policy and plan adopted in writing
summary: Council formally adopted an asset management policy, strategy and plan, a condition of an FCM asset-management grant and of new provincial requirements. Members said the city had long practised asset management and the document would guide 5- and 10-year capital funding.
status_detail: Discussed at the Sept 12, 2023 Strategic Priorities Committee (not recorded); adopted Oct 3, 2023 (R23-199). The plan itself is not presented in public meetings in detail.
reasons: study-first: Puts existing practice in writing with an asset inventory for future capital planning. (Jac Siemens)

title: Development fees to rise 5% a year (2024-2027), not the 7.5% staff recommended
summary: Staff proposed combining three fee by-laws and raising residential, non-residential and water/sewer impact fees 7.5% a year for four years, saying 2.5% annual increases since 2012 had fallen behind construction inflation. Michael Zwaagstra amended it to 5%, matching construction inflation, citing housing affordability and fees below Winkler, Morden, Brandon and Niverville. Damian Penner and Jake Hiebert voted against all three readings, arguing that 5% leaves existing taxpayers subsidizing growth through the mill rate. The mayor said council should have reviewed the fees sooner.
status_detail: By-law 2233 passed 5-2 at all three readings (R23-211 Oct 17; R23-224 and R23-225 Nov 7, 2023). Fees rise 5% a year 2024-2027 (staff wanted 7.5%); a review is due in 2027.
figures: Previous increases 2.5%/yr since 2012; construction inflation ~5-6%/yr; staff options 2.5%, 5%, 7.5%, 10%; staff note said ~11% over 4 years needed to restore past contribution levels (transcript Oct 17, 2023 0:08:47; Nov 7, 2023 0:06:44). Development fees collected 2022: ~$1.8-1.9M vs $615,000 budgeted (May 16, 2023).
reasons: ability-to-pay: Every increase is passed to home buyers; err on the side of affordability; need more homes. (Michael Zwaagstra); ability-to-pay: Would not have supported 7.5%; other governments are trying to make housing affordable. (Susan Penner); ability-to-pay: Entry-level housing would be hit hardest by 7.5%; tie increases to inflation. (Earl Funk); growth-pays: Fees buy access to existing water, sewer and streets; too big an increase could hurt growth; review in 2027. (Jac Siemens); growth-pays: Against 5%: existing residents on fixed incomes subsidize growth through the mill rate; has been falling behind since 2012. (Damian Penner); growth-pays: Against 5%: developers profit while taxpayers pay the difference; unfair. (Jake Hiebert)
public: No public hearing was required; no residents spoke.
seconder: J. Siemens (1st), B. Hiebert (2nd), S. Penner (3rd)
vote: 5-2 (against: Damian Penner, Jake Hiebert) at each reading
notes: The Sept 12, 2023 Strategic Priorities Committee meeting where 7.5% was first favoured was not recorded; accounts of it come from members' remarks.

title: Applications for provincial and federal project grants (MEDIP, Water Services Board, GRO, FCM)
summary: Council applied for cost-shared grants: three 2023 MEDIP projects (Hespeler Street, Hanover Street, fire hall floor/exhaust), 50% of design costs for the Lift Station 1 to lagoon force-main twinning from the Manitoba Water Services Board, two 2024 GRO projects (First Street surface works, outdoor pool renewal), disaster assistance after the Sept 2024 rain, and an FCM grant for a climate risk plan. Each commits matching city money.
status_detail: All applications approved unanimously; outcomes were not reported at council meetings in this period. Water Services Board funding for force-main work was being drawn on by 2025-2026 (later transcripts).
figures: MEDIP Hespeler St: $1.66M grant on $3.32M (R23-200); fire hall: $300,000 grant on $400,000 (R23-202); Hanover St amount not in parsed minutes. GRO First St: $990,000 on $1.98M (R24-217); outdoor pool: $937,500 on $1.875M (R24-218). MWSB 50% of design (R24-127). DFA request (R24-214). FCM climate adaptation (R24-242).
reasons: partner-money: If the city doesn't apply for dedicated provincial funding it won't get it. (Damian Penner)
notes: 2024-11-05 meeting (GRO, DFA) has no recording; minutes only. Hanover Street MEDIP amount not captured in the parsed motion text.

title: Supplementary taxes from new construction now budgeted to hold the line
summary: Council added $1.376M in 2023 supplementary taxes (Dec 2023) and $713,615 in 2024 (Nov 2024). Members stressed this was not new spending money because the city now budgets for it; in the 2024 budget debate Jac Siemens said budgeting this former 'found money' had been one way to hold taxes in past years, leaving less cushion.
status_detail: 2023 additions (R23-246) and cancellations (R23-247) Dec 5, 2023; 2024 additions (R24-229) and cancellations (R24-230) Nov 19, 2024; all unanimous.
figures: Added $1,375,974.97 and cancelled $113,247.53 (2023); added $713,614.82 and cancelled $58,062.27 (2024) (minutes). Budgeted: $550,000 (2023), $675,000 (2024) (staff presentations).
reasons: already-low-taxes: Budgeting supplementary taxes helped hold taxes but removed wiggle room. (Jac Siemens)
notes: The 2023 amount added ($1.376M) is well above the $550,000 the 2023 budget expected; how the difference was used was not explained at the meeting.

title: Interim 2024 budget and an $8M operating line of credit, up from about $5M
summary: As every year, council adopted an interim operating budget and a bank borrowing resolution to cover spending until the 2024 plan passed. Because of the Event Centre and PTH 12/Loewen projects, the mayor raised the fiscal-services line from $3M to $10M and the line of credit was set at $8M instead of the usual ~$5M.
status_detail: Interim budget (R23-244) and RBC borrowing up to $8M during 2024 (R23-245) carried unanimously.
figures: Fiscal services $10M (amended from $3M); line of credit $8M vs ~$5M before (transcript Dec 5, 2023 0:12:42, 0:16:15; minutes R23-244, R23-245).
notes: Routine yearly item; recorded for the size change.

title: Event Centre rises to $69.153M; $8.153M change order and $8.5M funding package approved
summary: After a year-long redesign failed to keep the Event Centre at $61M (soil conditions forced a structural floor; steel and mechanical savings fell through), staff recommended an $8.153M change order. Council funded $8.5M from the operating fund ($1.55M), new provincial money ($3.6M), the land and building reserve ($850,000) and $2.5M of the contingency borrowing, bringing the city's share to $30.675M. Members said cutting components would have put government and donor funding at risk.
status_detail: Funding sources (R23-252) and change order (R23-253) carried unanimously Dec 19, 2023. Progress billings reached $32.1M (46.5%) by Apr 2024 and nearly $50M by Oct 2024; the building neared completion by Nov 2024.
figures: Budget $61M -> $69.153M; change order $8.153M; funding $1,550,000 operating + $3,600,000 provincial (incl. $1M dedicated capital grant) + $850,000 L&B reserve + $2,500,000 debt = $8.5M; city share $30.675M; governments $18.5M; private donors $25.5M (transcript Dec 19, 2023 0:21:50, 0:32:15; minutes R23-252). Progress billings $32.1M / 46.5% (Apr 16, 2024 0:18:29-0:19:33); ~$50M (Oct 1, 2024 0:15:38).
reasons: partner-money: Removing components could jeopardize government and private funding tied to the full project. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Contingency borrowing was pre-approved; only half used. (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: City taxpayers pay less than half of a $69M facility. (Jac Siemens)
notes: The existing report puts the total near $74M including items outside the construction contract; this file uses the construction budget presented on Dec 19, 2023.

title: Lift Station 2 and Barkman Avenue debt issued at 5.41% over 5 years
summary: Council gave readings to debt-issue by-laws borrowing $2M (Lift Station 2) and $1.12M (Barkman Avenue water renewal) from TD Bank at 5.41% for 5 years, lower than the 8% ceiling but well above the ~2% the city was used to.
status_detail: First/second readings Dec 19, 2023 (R23-262 to R23-265); third readings Mar 5, 2024 after Municipal Board approval (R24-055, R24-056).
figures: $2M and $1.12M at 5.41%, 5 years, TD Bank; RBC quoted 5.5% (transcript Dec 19, 2023 0:51:25; Mar 5, 2024 0:47:38).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: The city doesn't always have the cash, so it borrows short-term for finished work. (Jake Hiebert)

title: 2024 financial plan: 5.1% tax increase to 14.4 mills, 'our toughest budget'
themes: budget; mill-rate; debt; capital-plan; event-centre; policing-cost
summary: After the mayor warned in Sept 2023 that rising interest rates and project costs meant council must 'rethink' at its study sessions, the 2024 plan raised the city mill rate about 5.1% to 14.4, with $38.5M in revenue and a $62.7M capital program (Event Centre completion, PTH 12/Loewen, Lift Station 2, Hanover Street). Members blamed construction inflation, higher interest and policing costs, said they would not cut services or infrastructure renewal, and said some renewal projects were pushed into later years. No one from the public spoke. Adopted unanimously (Susan Penner absent).
status_detail: Financial plan adopted Apr 2, 2024 (R24-073); tax levy By-law 2247 readings Apr 16 and May 7, 2024 (R24-089, R24-097, R24-098). Typical city tax bill rose to just over $120 a month.
figures: Mill rate 14.4, up just over 5% (transcript Apr 2, 2024 0:05:52); assessment growth 4.4%; revenue/expenses ~$38.5M; $19.8M from property taxes ($18.7M via mill rate); average home ~$225,000, city tax just over $120/month; supplementary taxes $675,000; per-capita grant $4.6M; grants to organizations just over $1M; labour $11.2M; protective services $5.1M; capital $62.7M; $16M new debt (Event Centre, PTH 12/Loewen), $1.5M repaid; average interest just under 4.2%; year-end debt ~$19.5M; debt payments $1.7M = 1.27 mills (~9% of rate); utility +4%, garbage +2.6%, permits +5%, land use fees +2.5%; out-years $20.1M, $5M, $16.1M (staff presentation 0:05:52-0:16:32). School levies on the tax by-law: Hanover SD 12.74 mills, provincial ESL 8.128 mills (May 7, 2024 0:12:44).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Not willing to sacrifice services or the infrastructure program; increase mainly from construction inflation. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Higher interest on loans; still repaying all debt in 5 years, including the Event Centre. (Michael Zwaagstra); already-low-taxes: Past tax holds relied on budgeting supplementary taxes; little wiggle room left. (Jac Siemens); infrastructure-first: Didn't want to repeat the indoor-pool era, when renewal was restricted for 5 years. (Jac Siemens); provincial-responsibility: City now pays a much larger share of RCMP costs. (Jac Siemens); dont-burden-future: Kicking renewal down the road creates bigger costs; temporary increases to keep the 5-year rule. (Damian Penner); efficiency: Wants deferred to later budgets; council 'gave up weekends' to build it. (Earl Funk)
reason_tags: already-low-taxes; dont-burden-future; efficiency; infrastructure-first; pay-as-you-go; provincial-responsibility
public: No one spoke at the public hearing (transcript Apr 2, 2024 0:17:05).
notes: Susan Penner was excused on Apr 2, 2024. J. Hiebert's spoken school-levy figures at 0:46:45 (Apr 16) are garbled; the City Manager's figures (May 7) are used. First raised Sept 19, 2023 (mayor calls for a rethink); dated here by the Apr 2, 2024 hearing.

title: Fee schedules updated on a cost-recovery basis; tax certificate fee $25 to $45
summary: Council accepted the 2024 and 2025 fee schedules (most fees escalate roughly with CPI, 2.5-3%) and raised the tax certificate fee from $25 to $45, the first change in 17 years. The 2025 schedule raised the development-agreement registration fee to $1,250 (last changed 2017). Members said fees are for cost recovery, not revenue.
status_detail: 2024 schedule accepted May 7, 2024 (R24-094); By-law 2243 passed May 7, 2024 (R24-095, R24-096); 2025 schedule accepted Dec 17, 2024 (R24-254).
figures: Tax certificate fee $25 -> $45; 400-700 issued a year (transcript May 7, 2024 0:10:48, 0:11:27); fee escalation 2.5-3% average; registration fee to $1,250 (Dec 17, 2024 0:53:31). 2024 budget: permit fees +5%, land-use fees +2.5%.
reasons: efficiency: Fees should recover the cost of services. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: M. Zwaagstra (fee schedules); J. Siemens, S. Penner (By-law 2243)
seconder: D. Penner; J. Hiebert, M. Zwaagstra; J. Siemens

title: Province previews 2025 reassessment: Steinbach values up about 12.7%
summary: A provincial assessor told council values would rise about 12.7% on average for 2025 and that higher assessments need not mean higher taxes if council adjusts the mill rate. He also explained the 50% school tax rebate now applied directly on tax bills. Council asked only technical questions. The 2025 roll was accepted on the Board of Revision's recommendation in Nov 2024. (In 2025 council held the rate at 14.4, so revenue rose with assessments; outside this period.)
status_detail: Presentation received Jun 18, 2024; 2025 assessment roll accepted Nov 5, 2024 (R24-216, J. Siemens/D. Penner). Board of Revision members (residents) reappointed Oct 17, 2023.
figures: Average increase 12.7%; taxable assessment +14.2% vs 13% provincially; school tax rebate 50% for residential/farm, 10% other (transcript Jun 18, 2024 1:01:17-1:15:04). Previous reassessment growth 8.3%.
public: Provincial assessor (R.S., Manitoba Municipal Assessment Services) presented.
notes: The 2025 assessment roll decision (Nov 5, 2024) has no recording.

title: $7.5M Event Centre loan arranged at 3.8% over 5 years
summary: Council gave first and second reading to By-law 2256, borrowing the full $7.5M authorized in 2022 for the Event Centre from RBC at 3.8% for 5 years, with first payment due end of 2025. Members said the facility would be debt-free in five years.
status_detail: First and second readings Dec 17, 2024 (R24-255, R24-256); third reading to follow Municipal Board approval (2025, outside this period). Whether the separate $2.5M contingency draw was issued as debt was not found in 2024 records.
figures: $7.5M, RBC, 3.8%, 5 years, original ceiling 7% under By-law 2186 (transcript Dec 17, 2024 0:58:22).
reasons: dont-burden-future: Paid off in 5 years so the Event Centre is debt-free. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Event Centre operating agreement: city pays 0.5 mills (about $700,000) a year to the operator
summary: Council signed a 3-year operating agreement with the Southeast Events Group (SEG) to run the new Southeast Event Centre. The city gives SEG an annual operating grant equal to 0.5 mills of the municipal levy (about $700,000) to Dec 31, 2029, plus a one-time pre-opening grant of up to $600,000, and keeps approval of SEG's annual budgets. Zwaagstra called a subsidy normal for a recreation facility; at the Mar 4, 2025 hearing Susan Penner asked that the Event Centre's operating cost be shown in the grants line so its cost is visible.
status_detail: Agreement approved unanimously (R25-003). The grant is in the 2025 and 2026 budgets; the 2025 Parks and Rec increase (about $800,000 per staff; S. Penner cited $850,000) included Event Centre operating money. Whether the grant was moved to a separate grants line, as S. Penner asked, was not reported in a meeting.
figures: 0.5 mills = about $700,000/yr to Dec 31, 2029; one-time pre-opening grant up to $600,000; first term to Feb 14, 2028 (minutes Jan 7, 2025, item 6; transcript 0:06:13).
reasons: recreation-subsidy: Recreation facilities cost money to run, so a city subsidy is normal; agreed in the 2019 memorandum of understanding. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: The exact grant amount in each year depends on the value of one mill; $700,000 is the city's estimate.

title: Interim operating budgets and operating lines of credit (routine)
summary: Each December/January council adopts an interim operating budget so the city can pay its bills until the financial plan is passed, and authorizes short-term operating borrowing from the Royal Bank. The authorized operating credit fell from up to $8 million for 2025 to up to $2 million for 2026.
