status_detail: All carried unanimously: R25-005 and R25-007 (Jan 7, 2025); R25-238 and R25-241 (Dec 2, 2025). Routine.
figures: Operating borrowing authority: up to $8,000,000 for 2025 (R25-007); up to $2,000,000 for 2026 (R25-241) (minutes).
mover: Jac Siemens (R25-005); Jake Hiebert (R25-007); Damian Penner (R25-238, R25-241)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R25-005, R25-238, R25-241); Bill Hiebert (R25-007)
notes: Grouped routine yearly items.

title: RCMP costs: council protests federal bargaining it pays for but doesn't control
summary: Steinbach pays 90% of the cost of its 18 contracted RCMP officers, but wages are bargained by the federal government. Council sent a letter (AMM template) asking for a say in the third round of RCMP bargaining after a 23.7% retroactive raise in the last round. At the 2025 hearing staff said policing rose about $400,000, set by the RCMP's own budget.
status_detail: Letter authorized unanimously (R25-008). No federal response was reported at a later meeting. Policing cost rose about $400,000 in the 2025 budget; protective services budgeted at $5.6M (2025) and $5.9M (2026).
figures: City pays 90% of RCMP contract cost for 18 officers; last round 23.7% retroactive raise (transcript Jan 7, 2025 0:20:23); policing +$400,000 in 2025 (Mar 4, 2025 0:15:17); protective services $5.6M (2025), $5.9M (2026) (financial plan presentations).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: RCMP pay is set in federal bargaining; the city only chooses the number of officers, so costs are outside its control. (Michael Zwaagstra); provincial-responsibility: A higher level of government is spending the city's money without consulting it. (Susan Penner)

title: Garbage fee and other user fees raised in small yearly steps on a cost-recovery basis
summary: Council renewed the residential curbside garbage special service levy for 2025-2027 at $162, $168 and $174 a year (from $155), on a cost-recovery basis. The 2025 and 2026 budgets also raised utility (water/sewer) rates about 3% a year, permit fees 5% and land-use application fees 2.5%, and council accepted the 2026 fee schedule.
status_detail: By-Law 2257 first/second reading Feb 4, 2025 (R25-027, R25-028), third reading Jun 17, 2025 after Municipal Board review (R25-132); 2026 fee schedule accepted Dec 16, 2025 (R25-259). All unanimous. No utility rate by-law debate was found in the meetings searched; the 3% figures come from the budget presentations.
reasons: cost-recovery: Fees track rising costs; service unchanged. (Michael Zwaagstra); efficiency: $162 a year for garbage pickup is good value. (Damian Penner)
public: No one spoke at the Feb 4, 2025 hearing (minutes).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R25-027); Damian Penner (R25-028); Susan Penner (R25-132); Bill Hiebert (R25-259)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R25-027, R25-259); Jac Siemens (R25-028); Damian Penner (R25-132)

title: Lift Station 1 and lagoon force main twinning: $6.6M, partly borrowed over 5 years
summary: Council approved Local Improvement Plan 2025-01 to twin the 3-km force main from Lift Station 1 to the lagoon and upgrade the lift station. Of about $6.6M, up to $2.75M is borrowed over 5 years (budgeted at up to 7%), with the rest from the utility reserve, utility operating fund and an expected grant; council asked the Manitoba Water Services Board (MWSB) for 50%. Contracts followed in 2025-26: a $670,600 generator, the Park Road West force main ($1.49M) and the Lift Station 1 upgrade ($4.33M).
status_detail: By-Law 2255 first/second reading Feb 4, 2025 (R25-025, R25-026), MWSB request Feb 18 (R25-038), Municipal Board approval and third reading Jul 2, 2025 (R25-137). Contracts awarded: generator R25-210, force main R26-038, lift station R26-060 (all unanimous). The Mar 17, 2026 tender report says funding includes an MWSB grant.
figures: Project $6.595M; borrowing max $2.75M over 5 years at max 7%, about $670,700/yr; 0.488 mills, under $50/yr on a $250,000 home (Feb 4, 2025 0:05:25); generator $670,600 (R25-210); Park Road West force main $1,494,661.05 (R26-038); Lift Station 1 upgrades $4,326,078.39, pumping 482 to 843 L/s (R26-060; Mar 17, 2026 1:53:20).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Sewer capacity is the core job; nearby communities have had growth stall. (Susan Penner); pay-as-you-go: Borrowed portion repaid in 5 years under the usual policy. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No one spoke at the Feb 4, 2025 public hearing; no written objections (minutes).
mover: Susan Penner (R25-025); Jac Siemens (R25-026, R25-038); Michael Zwaagstra (R25-137)
seconder: Jac Siemens (R25-025); Bill Hiebert (R25-026); Jake Hiebert (R25-038); Susan Penner (R25-137)
notes: The MWSB grant amount for this project was not stated in the meetings searched.

title: Council asks the province to quadruple Manitoba Water Services Board funding; seeks 50% grants for sewer projects
summary: Council backed a Manitoba Municipal Administrators resolution asking the province to raise the Manitoba Water Services Board capital budget from $24M to $100M, noting it was oversubscribed 56 times ($1.35B requested). It also asked MWSB for 50% of its own Lift Station 1/force main and Millwork Drive sewer projects.
status_detail: Resolutions R25-038, R25-193 and R25-258 carried unanimously. 2026 tender reports list an MWSB grant among funding sources for Lift Station 1 and Millwork Drive; no provincial increase to the MWSB budget was reported.
figures: MWSB $24M/yr, $1.35B requested, oversubscribed 56x; ask $100M; 103 municipalities unfunded (Funk, Oct 7, 2025 0:26:10-0:28:55).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Municipalities can't afford $100M+ water projects alone; growth stops without servicing. (Susan Penner); provincial-responsibility: The province can't afford growing communities having to stop development. (Mayor Earl Funk)
mover: Jac Siemens (R25-038); Michael Zwaagstra (R25-193); Susan Penner (R25-258)
notes: MWSB grant amounts received were not stated in the meetings searched.

title: Chamber of Commerce's share of the business tax: review and cap promised, not done
summary: The city levies a 0.5% business tax and passes it, less a 5% administration fee, to the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce (about $225,000 in 2025). Susan Penner called the amount 'way out of line' because it grows automatically with assessments, and the mayor agreed it should be reviewed at a study session. A year later council passed the 2026 business tax levy unchanged; S. Penner and D. Penner again said the automatic growth may need a cap, while the mayor praised the Chamber partnership.
status_detail: Business tax by-laws passed unanimously in 2025 (By-Law 2264) and 2026 (By-Law 2277) at 0.5%. No change, cap or public result of the study-session review was reported by Nov 2026.
figures: Business tax 0.5% of business assessment, less 5% admin fee, to the Chamber; about $225,000 (S. Penner, Mar 4, 2025 0:19:31); Winkler's chamber gets $65,000 (S. Penner, same turn; not verified).
reasons: business-supports-it: Businesses have asked to keep the tax when council considered cancelling it. (Susan Penner); partnership: The Chamber partnership has grown into a strong advocacy relationship. (Mayor Earl Funk)
mover: Susan Penner (R25-084, R26-073, R26-087); Jake Hiebert (R25-097, R26-088); Jac Siemens (R25-098)
seconder: Jac Siemens (R25-084); Michael Zwaagstra (R25-097, R26-088); Bill Hiebert (R25-098, R26-087); Jake Hiebert (R26-073)
notes: The $225,000 amount and Winkler comparison are as stated by S. Penner; not checked against the budget package.

title: 2025 financial plan: mill rate held at 14.4 in a reassessment year, so city tax revenue rose 14.8%
themes: budget; mill-rate; reassessment; debt; reserves; capital-plan
summary: In a reassessment year when values rose 14.9%, council kept the rate at 14.4 mills instead of lowering it as in past reassessment years, so property-tax revenue rose 14.8% (about $2.9M); staff estimated about 11 points of that came from reassessment. Debt payments (+$1.35M), policing (+$400,000), parks and rec including the Event Centre (+$800,000) and public works (+$300,000) drove it. Councillors called it their toughest budget, said reserves were low after Event Centre overruns, refused to stretch debt beyond 5 years, and put $5M back into reserves. Resident G.S. asked whether infrastructure renewal is keeping up.
status_detail: Approved in principle Mar 4, 2025 (R25-048, 5 members present; B. Hiebert and Siemens excused) and adopted in full Apr 15, 2025 once school taxes were known (R25-082). Tax levy By-Law 2263 and business tax By-Law 2264 passed Apr 15 and May 6. All unanimous.
figures: Mill rate 14.4 (unchanged); assessment growth 14.9%; property-tax revenue +14.8% (~$2.9M), of which ~3.5% real growth; $22.7M from property taxes ($21.6M via mill rate); revenue/expenses just over $42M; capital $36.6M; new debt $13.25M, $2.6M retired; debt payments $3.1M incl. $443,000 interest = 1.945 mills (13.5% of city rate); year-end debt ~$21.5M; average home ~$250,000 pays ~$135/month city tax; grants to groups just over $1M; labour $12M; future capital $18.2M, $58.2M, $56.5M (Mar 4, 2025 0:03:33-0:15:17). Combined residential rate incl. education 26.76 mills (Apr 15, 2025 0:26:52). $5M to reserves (D. Penner 0:42:05).
reasons: infrastructure-first: Won't cut or delay infrastructure to avoid the increase; infrastructure is a city's first priority. (Michael Zwaagstra); reserves-low: Reserves were spent on Event Centre overruns, so less is available to fund work without tax. (Michael Zwaagstra); reserves-low: Years of holding the line drew reserves down to an uncomfortable level; $5M goes back into reserves. (Damian Penner); efficiency: No frivolous spending; council runs a tight ship; construction costs have doubled or tripled. (Susan Penner); dont-burden-future: Stretching debt to lower this year's increase would cost more and burden future councils. (Michael Zwaagstra); ability-to-pay: Dislikes tax increases; looked for adjustments with the finance manager but found none. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: G.S. (resident) asked how the city ensures infrastructure isn't falling behind, noting that the book value of city infrastructure declined relative to original cost from 2010 to 2022 in the audited statements. The City Manager replied that the city keeps a 7-10 year capital plan, uses engineering models, and its streets rated 72/100 in the latest pavement review.
notes: Only five members were present for the Mar 4 vote.

title: Council debates and keeps its rule of repaying all debt within 5 years
summary: At the 2025 hearing Zwaagstra asked staff whether longer borrowing would cut this year's increase; staff said yes in the short run but residents would pay more over time. Council kept the 5-year rule (a practice dating from the 1980s, not a by-law). Zwaagstra said a big wastewater project may make the rule hard to keep; in 2026 Damian Penner called it best practice that makes Steinbach 'the envy' of other cities.
status_detail: Rule kept in the 2025 and 2026 plans ('The city continues to use a 5-year amortization term for all of its debt', staff, Mar 17, 2026). No written debt policy was adopted; how the wastewater plant will be financed was not decided by Nov 2026.
figures: 2025: debt payments $3.1M incl. $443,000 interest, 1.945 mills (13.5% of city rate); 2026: $3.9M incl. $556,000 interest, 2.427 mills (just under 17%); average rate just over 4% (Mar 4, 2025 0:11:50; Mar 17, 2026 0:27:39). 2012: 10% tax increase mostly to a new recreation reserve, about $800,000/yr (Zwaagstra, Mar 18, 2025 0:05:33).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: Short debt carries lower interest and costs less overall. (Michael Zwaagstra); dont-burden-future: Longer debt hands today's projects to future councils and leaves less room for necessary work. (Michael Zwaagstra); pay-as-you-go: Interest is significant even on 5-year terms; keep debt minimal and short. (Damian Penner)
notes: The rule is described by council as a policy since the 1980s; no written by-law was cited.

title: Does growth pay for itself? Council says no; supplementary taxes are small and already budgeted
summary: Defending the 2025 increase, Zwaagstra said 'the old maxim that growth pays for itself is not true': growth drives the Event Centre, highway, sewer and RCMP costs. Supplementary taxes on new buildings ($876,457 added in 2025, $100,305 cancelled) are mostly budgeted in advance, so 'there is no windfall'; in 2026 Susan Penner called $730,000 a year small relative to growth. Capital development fees exceeded budget in 2024 (about $3M to reserves). Council did not change development charges in this period.
status_detail: Supplementary taxes added and cancelled (R25-239, R25-240, unanimous). No change to capital development fees or a growth-cost study was brought to council in 2025-2026; the next renewal of the development fee schedule was not discussed in the meetings searched.
figures: Supplementary taxes budgeted $675,000 (2025), $730,000 (2026) (financial plans); $876,457.09 added and $100,304.77 cancelled for 2025 (R25-239, R25-240); ~$3M of 2024 capital development fees to land and building reserve (Jun 17, 2025); permit values ~$105M (2024), $118M (2025) (financial plans).
reasons: growth-pays: Growth does not pay for itself; it forces new facilities, roads, sewer capacity and policing. (Michael Zwaagstra); growth-pays: Supplementary taxes are a small addition to the tax base relative to the volume of growth. (Susan Penner)
notes: Whether higher development charges were considered in study sessions is unknown (sessions are not recorded).

title: Provincial and federal money in the budget: about $6M a year plus policing and safety grants
summary: Staff reported the provincial per-capita tax-sharing grant at $4.6M (2025) and $4.8M (2026) and the federal gas tax at just over $1M a year, used partly for the asphalt program. The province also paid a final 2025 operating-grant instalment of $542,952, an urban policing grant of about $2.6M a year (up 2% for 2026-27), and an unexpected $200,000 public safety grant in 2026. Council received these as information.
status_detail: Received as information; CCBF (gas tax) expenditure report for 2024 accepted (R25-166). No council debate on a provincial grant freeze was found in this period.
figures: Per-capita grant $4.6M (2025), $4.8M (2026); gas tax just over $1M (Mar 4, 2025 0:06:04; Mar 17, 2026 0:08:40); final 2025 operating grant payment $542,952.29 (minutes Oct 7, 2025); urban policing grant just over $2.6M (Dec 2, 2025 0:17:28; Oct 20, 2026 0:39:02); $200,000 public safety grant (Jul 21, 2026 1:22:18).
notes: How the $200,000 safety grant was finally allocated was not checked.

title: City ends its $65,000-a-year economic development office grant
summary: Since 2021 the city matched funding of $65,000 a year for an economic development office (Steinbach Economic Development, under the Chamber of Commerce) as a 5-year pilot. In March 2025 SED presented and asked for more funding, which was sent to the July study session. In August 2025 council voted not to renew the grant after Dec 31, 2025, saying it had not seen results and that the Chamber and local business people already do the work.
status_detail: R25-158 carried unanimously: the city 'does not renew its grant funding commitment' after Dec 31, 2025 (minutes).
reasons: value-for-money: Hasn't seen the development hoped for; the office changed CEOs and vision. (Jac Siemens); value-for-money: Both Hieberts said they had campaigned for an economic development office but saw no measurable results and duplication with the Chamber. (Bill Hiebert / Jake Hiebert (turns not separable)); partnership: Economic development is a team effort of council, Chamber, developers and the CDC, not one office. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Steinbach Economic Development (organization) presented its work on Mar 18, 2025 and requested more funding.
notes: The two Hiebert speakers (labels C and F) are low confidence in the speaker map, so they are not quoted by name.

title: Funding requests from groups go to unrecorded budget study sessions
summary: City grants to organizations total about $1M (2025) and $1.1M (2026). Most new requests were 'received as information' or referred to the summer or fall budget study session, which is not public: Eastman Raiders field lights (May 2025), Steinbach Economic Development (Mar 2025), a Southeast Events Group funding request (Jun 2026), a Grand Slam of Curling host fee of $20,000 a year for 3 years and a grant in lieu of taxes for the Cafe House (both Oct 2026). Some were granted in public: $15,000 to the Sports Heritage Committee, an Arts Council increase, and tax receipts for Golf Club donations.
status_detail: Granted: Sports Heritage $15,000 (R25-236), Arts Council increase (thank-you letter Sept 16, 2025), Golf Club donation receipts (R26-144). Referred with no public result found: Raiders lights, SED (later ended, see 2025-economic-development-grant-ended), SEG request, Grand Slam host fee, Cafe House.
figures: Grants to groups just over $1M (2025), just over $1.1M (2026) (financial plans); Sports Heritage $15,000 (R25-236); Grand Slam $20,000/yr x 3 to unlock $150,000-$160,000/yr in outside funding (Funk, Oct 20, 2026 0:39:02); Raiders lights operating $120-$200/month (delegation, May 6, 2025).
reasons: process: Budget items are decided together at the study session where the budget is built. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Eastman Raiders (football club) asked for floodlights; Southeast Events Group, Cafe House and Steinbach Economic Development made written or in-person requests.
notes: Study sessions are not recorded, so outcomes of referred requests could not be verified.

title: Wastewater treatment expansion: $132.5M funding application; city share at least $65.4M; cost estimate later 'over $200 million'
summary: Council ratified an application to the federal Canada Housing Infrastructure Fund for 50% of a $132.5M project (new treatment facility about $94M, Lift Station 1 / force main about $8M, a new west lift station and trunk sewer about $30M) and committed to fund the remaining $65.4M. Staff said joining the regional RSR wastewater co-op was 25-30% costlier and would have meant ceding land, so the city goes alone. In May 2026 Susan Penner said projected costs had 'skyrocketed to over $200 million' and urged council to challenge provincial requirements. No funding decision or financing plan was reported by Nov 2026.
status_detail: Application ratified (R25-081, unanimous). Staff planned a further application to a joint federal-provincial stream. No grant announcement, final cost or borrowing plan was reported at council through Oct 20, 2026; Zwaagstra had said the project may make the 5-year debt rule hard to keep.
figures: Eligible cost $132,475,000; 50% requested; city share $65,447,500 (minutes R25-081); components ~$94M treatment, ~$8M lift station/force main, ~$30M west lift station and 1.5-km gravity main (Warkentin, Apr 15, 2025 0:15:25); RSR co-op 25-30% costlier; needed in 7-8 years (Siemens 0:23:23); 'over $200 million' (S. Penner, May 5, 2026 0:00:12).
reasons: partner-money: Hoping other governments cover 50% or more; still a significant budget impact. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Must not end up like Morden, which has had a development stop since 2020. (Mayor Earl Funk); efficiency: Costs driven by regulation, complexity and approvals; ask the province for outcome-based standards. (Susan Penner)
notes: S. Penner calls it a 'water treatment facility/plant'; from context she means the wastewater treatment project. The 'over $200 million' figure was not presented by staff in the meetings searched.

title: Library raises non-resident fee 50%; city raises library support
summary: At council's request the Jake Epp Library board reviewed its fees and raised the non-resident fee from $110 to $165 a year, citing wage and book cost increases and that 35-40% of users live outside Steinbach while residents pay through property taxes. City support for the library rose from $455,000 (2025) to $515,000 (2026).
status_detail: Fee set by the library board (effective July 1, 2025), reported to council by Siemens; the 2026 budget funded the library 'at the increased level that we had agreed upon last year' (Zwaagstra).
figures: Non-resident fee $110 to $165/yr; minimum wages up ~40%, book costs up 60%+ (Siemens, May 6, 2025 1:20:46); library support $455,000 (2025), $515,000 (2026) (financial plan presentations).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Non-residents should pay similar to what residents pay through property taxes, as at the pool and arena. (Jac Siemens)
vote: not recorded (library board decision received as information)
notes: 'JCAT' is the transcript's rendering of Jake Epp.

title: Private overnight security patrol paid from unspent RCMP money, then budgeted
summary: Because Steinbach was getting about 14 to 15 of the 18 RCMP officers it pays for, council in June 2025 hired a private overnight patrol funded from the unspent policing budget. In November 2025 it continued the pilot and put about $145,000 into the 2026 budget for consideration. When the provider closed in October 2026, council awarded a replacement contract (about $148,000 for 2027).
status_detail: R25-118 (Jun 17, 2025) and R25-209 (Nov 4, 2025) carried unanimously; Oct 20, 2026 contract to Next Level Servicing Corp. carried (no minutes available yet for that meeting; vote from transcript).
figures: RCMP short 15-25% of 18 paid positions (Zwaagstra, Jun 17, 2025 0:07:37); 2026 cost about $145,000 (Nov 4, 2025 0:04:32); 2027 preliminary budget $150,000, contract $380/night, about $148,000 incl. PST (Oct 20, 2026 0:19:56).
reasons: efficiency: Costs less than one RCMP officer for extra overnight coverage. (Michael Zwaagstra); no-new-money: Paid by reallocating money already budgeted for the RCMP. (Susan Penner)
public: Developers and business owners had raised property-crime concerns with council (as described by council members); the RCMP and developers reported a positive effect (staff report).
resolution_no: R25-118; R25-209; Oct 20, 2026 contract (no minutes yet)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R25-118, R25-209); a Councillor Penner (Oct 20, 2026, per transcript)
seconder: Susan Penner (R25-118, R25-209); Jac Siemens (Oct 20, 2026, per transcript)
notes: Oct 20, 2026 mover is 'Councillor Penner' in the transcript; which Penner is not certain without minutes.

title: 2024 year-end: $8.5M moved to reserves, $3M more than planned from development fees
summary: Ratifying the 2024 reserve transfers, staff reported $8.5M moved to reserves against $5.5M budgeted, including nearly $3M to the land and building reserve (budget $1M) from extra capital development fees. Councillors said reserves make the 5-year borrowing rule possible. Council also accepted the 2024 audited statements.
status_detail: Reserve transfers R25-125 and 2024 audited financial reports R25-126 carried unanimously.
figures: Transfers to reserves $8.5M actual vs ~$5.5M budget; ~$3M to land and building reserve vs $1M budget (Warkentin, Jun 17, 2025 0:18:04-0:19:16).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: Without reserves the city could not keep to 5-year borrowing. (Damian Penner); pay-as-you-go: Reserves reduce future borrowing and allow projects otherwise not possible. (Susan Penner)
notes: The City Manager said 'December 31st, 2023' when introducing the audit; the minutes say the 2024 statements were accepted.

title: Event Centre and Loewen/PTH 12 borrowing: $13M of debentures, all on 5-year terms
summary: Council issued $7.5M (3.8%) and then $2.5M (3.83%) of 5-year debentures for the Southeast Event Centre, using $10M of the $12.5M it had authorized, and $3M (3.83%) for the city's share of the Loewen Boulevard/PTH 12 intersection, built with the province. Councillors noted rates came in near half the 7% budgeted and that the Event Centre will be debt-free by 2030.
status_detail: By-Law 2256 third reading Jul 2, 2025 (R25-139); By-Laws 2270 and 2271 first/second reading Dec 16, 2025 (R25-254 to R25-257) and third reading Feb 3, 2026 after Municipal Board approval (R26-028, R26-029). All unanimous.
figures: Event Centre: $12.5M authorized; $7.5M at 3.8% (Jul 2, 2025 0:26:20) + $2.5M at 3.83% (Dec 16, 2025 1:04:40) = $10M; total cost about $76M (Funk). Loewen/PTH 12: $3M at 3.83%, 5 years, budgeted $3.5M at 7% (Dec 16, 2025 1:02:16, 1:04:08); intersection about $14M (Funk, Mar 4, 2025).
reasons: pay-as-you-go: 5-year term is the normal policy; paid off by 2030. (Jac Siemens); partner-money: Loewen/PTH 12 done in partnership with the province; the city borrows only its share. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Jac Siemens (R25-139); Michael Zwaagstra (R25-254, R25-256, R26-028); Susan Penner (R25-255, R25-257); Damian Penner (R26-029)
seconder: Bill Hiebert (R25-139, R25-255, R25-257, R26-029); Jake Hiebert (R25-254); Susan Penner (R25-256); Jac Siemens (R26-028)

title: After two storms, flood and sewer-backup work moved up in the 2026 budget
summary: After basement flooding in Sept 2024 and Sept 2025, Susan Penner (herself flooded twice) demanded action 'now', not in the 5- or 10-year plan. Council held a November 2025 study session and the 2026 budget funded a flood mitigation plan: Lift Station 1, Park Road West force main and Millwork Drive sewer (about $8-9M), drainage on PTH 52 East and Park Road East, rerouting the Clear Spring Greens low-pressure sewer, and a sump-pump by-law review. The province declined Disaster Financial Assistance for the 2025 storm. Resident M.R. asked for a root-cause study.
status_detail: Projects funded in the 2026 plan (R26-058) and contracts awarded (R26-038, R26-050, R26-060, Park Road East low-pressure sewer R26-149). A climate risk assessment was due spring 2026; a root-cause study requested by residents was not reported as commissioned. Provincial DFA declined; follow-up requested.
figures: 126-135 mm in 4 hours on Sept 11-12, 2025 (Warkentin, Sept 16, 2025 0:41:04); three sewer projects about $8-9M (Mar 17, 2026 0:17:48); over $20M for wastewater in 2026 (D. Penner 0:38:22); Park Road East low-pressure sewer $396,500 vs $614,000 estimate (Jul 21, 2026 1:20:48).
reasons: infrastructure-first: If basic infrastructure doesn't work, nothing else matters. (Susan Penner); provincial-responsibility: Province declined disaster assistance for homeowners. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: M.R. (resident, Golfview Crescent, flooded more than 5 times) welcomed the reroute but asked whether consultants or engineers recommended it, when work would happen, and for a study of the root cause; staff said the reroute was council-initiated, not study-based.
notes: Flooding is also a topic in its own right; this action records only the budget and spending side.

title: Outdoor pool renewal: city applies twice for 50% provincial GROW funding
summary: Council applied to Manitoba's Growth, Renewal and Opportunities (GROW) program for half of an outdoor pool deck and equipment renewal, committing the city's half. Staff said the project had sat on the long-term capital plan for 10-12 years because recreation projects are hard to fund. In October 2026 council approved a second application for a larger estimate.
status_detail: R25-182 (Sep 16, 2025) carried unanimously; second application approved Oct 20, 2026 (transcript; minutes not yet available). No funding decision reported.
figures: 2025: $3,615,500 total, $1,807,750 requested, city commits $1,807,750 (R25-182). 2026: about $3.85M, $1.925M requested (Warkentin, Oct 20, 2026 0:34:46). Pool built about 1979 (Zwaagstra, same meeting).
reasons: partner-money: Renew before it costs more; outside money makes it possible. (Susan Penner)
notes: Whether the 2025 application was turned down (implied by the 2026 re-application) was not stated.

title: Landfill land and compactor bought from the environmental reserve, not taxes
summary: Council used the environmental reserve, built from landfill fees, to buy land next to the landfill at 148 Hanover Road East for $450,000 and, in October 2026, to buy a $1.33M landfill compactor a few months early after breakdowns. Councillors stressed neither purchase affects the mill rate.
status_detail: Land purchase R26-010 (Zwaagstra / J. Hiebert, unanimous); compactor approved Oct 20, 2026 (transcript; minutes not yet available).
figures: Land $450,000 (R26-010); compactor Tana H380 $1.329M plus taxes (Warkentin, Oct 20, 2026 0:30:48).
reasons: user-pays: Paid from landfill fees saved in the environmental reserve; no effect on the mill rate. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R26-010); a Councillor Hiebert (Oct 20, 2026, transcript)
notes: Oct 20, 2026 speakers are not mapped; members not quoted.

title: 2026 tenders come in under estimates; council credits early tendering
summary: Council awarded the 2026 capital works (asphalt and sidewalks, funded partly by federal gas tax and the capital development reserve), the Millwork Drive sewer renewal (about $700,000 under the $2.1M estimate), the Lift Station 1 upgrade, fire hall ventilation and equipment replacements. Members said early tendering produced lower bids and that savings go to reserves and future projects.
status_detail: Awarded unanimously: crawler R26-024, front-load truck R26-025, Park Road West force main R26-038, capital works R26-049, Millwork Drive R26-050, Lift Station 1 R26-060, fire hall ventilation R26-061.
figures: Capital works $1,379,680 (R26-049); Millwork Drive $1,462,540 vs estimate $2,129,607 (R26-050; Mar 3, 2026 0:10:41); Lift Station 1 $4,326,078.39 (single bid, below estimate) (R26-060); fire hall $367,025 vs $450,000 budget (R26-061); crawler net $520,000 (R26-024); front-load truck $516,699 vs $560,000 budget (R26-025).
reasons: efficiency: Tendering early and packaging projects brings better prices. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-first: Basic infrastructure is the most important thing the city does. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: 2026 financial plan: rate held at 14.4 mills, $35.8M capital, mostly sewer work
themes: budget; mill-rate; debt; capital-plan; wastewater; reserves
summary: With assessment growth of only 2.4%, council kept the rate at 14.4 mills and presented a 'zero tax increase budget': revenue just under $44M, capital $35.8M (over $20M for wastewater), $7.25M of new debt against $3.4M retired. Councillors credited early tendering, 5-year debt and reserves; Siemens noted bills can still rise with assessments. Mayor Funk later said Steinbach has one of the lowest mill rates in Manitoba.
status_detail: Approved in principle Mar 17, 2026 (R26-058, unanimous); tax levy By-Law 2276 passed Apr 7 and Apr 21 (R26-072, R26-085, R26-086). A separate final adoption resolution like 2025's R25-082 was not found in the 2026 minutes.
figures: Mill rate 14.4; assessment growth 2.4%; $23.4M from property taxes (53% of revenue); revenue/expenses just under $44M; capital $35.8M; supplementary taxes $730,000; grants to groups just over $1.1M; labour $12.8M; protective services $5.9M (18 RCMP, 53 firefighters); new debt $7.25M, retired $3.4M; year-end debt ~$16.7M; debt payments $3.9M incl. $556,000 interest = 2.427 mills (just under 17%); future capital $17.8M, $58.3M, $45.6M (Mar 17, 2026 0:08:40, 0:27:39).
reasons: already-low-taxes: One of the lowest mill rates and taxation in Manitoba. (Mayor Earl Funk); infrastructure-first: Infrastructure renewal is council's main priority; wastewater is the largest focus. (Damian Penner); efficiency: Early tendering brought projects in under budget, freeing money for reserves. (Damian Penner)
public: M.R. (resident) spoke on flood mitigation (see 2025-flood-mitigation-spending).
notes: The 2.4% figure is 'property value growth' as presented by staff; it is not a reassessment year.

title: $400,000 loan to the Event Centre operator, repaid over 4 years
summary: Because the Event Centre opened late and missed part of its first year, the Southeast Events Group asked for help with cash flow. Council passed a lending by-law for a $400,000 loan, repaid $100,000 a year from Sept 30, 2027, ahead of any surplus. Councillors stressed it is a loan, not a grant. SEG made a further funding request that was sent to the summer study session.
status_detail: By-Law 2272 first reading Jun 2 (R26-115), second and third readings Jun 16, 2026 (R26-125, R26-126), unanimous.
figures: $400,000; 4 annual payments of $100,000 from Sept 30, 2027 (Zwaagstra, Jun 16, 2026 0:39:07).
reasons: protect-city-asset: It's a city-owned facility; in the city's interest that it be on firm financial footing. (Michael Zwaagstra); repayable: A loan, repaid before surpluses are allocated. (Damian Penner)
mover: Damian Penner (R26-115); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-125); Bill Hiebert (R26-126)
notes: The interest rate on the loan was not stated in the meetings.

title: 2025 audited statements: spending within $100,000 of budget; auditor praises 5-year borrowing
summary: Council accepted the 2025 audited statements and ratified the 2025 reserve transfers. Damian Penner reported revenue of $68.3M (including utilities and grants) against operating expenses of $40.8M, with the difference going largely to reserves and capital, and expenses $100,000 under the $40.9M budget. The mayor said the auditor praised the 5-year borrowing rule. The audit meeting itself was not public.
status_detail: Audited reports accepted (R26-124, unanimous); reserve transfers approved by voice vote (no resolution number found in the minutes). Auditor: Reid & Miller re-appointed for 2025 at $62,000 (R25-191); Adeptus Advisory Group signed the 2025 report and was appointed for 2026 (R26-188).
figures: 2025 revenue $68.3M; expenses $40.8M vs $40.9M budget (D. Penner, Jun 16, 2026 0:34:47); audit fees $54,000 city + $4,500 library + $3,500 CDC = $62,000 for 2025 (Oct 7, 2025 0:16:42).
reasons: efficiency: Actual spending within $100,000 of budget shows administration knows what it takes to run the city. (Damian Penner)
notes: Whether Reid & Miller became Adeptus Advisory Group (which would explain the change of auditor name) was not verified.

title: 2027 reassessment: values up 9%; the new council sets the 2027 rate
summary: The provincial assessor reported that Steinbach's taxable assessment rises 9% ($131M) for 2027 (residential 12%, commercial 5%), and that with an unchanged city budget the average single-family home's taxes would rise about 3%. Whether to lower the mill rate as in most past reassessment years, or hold it as in 2025, is a decision for the council elected in Oct 2026.
status_detail: Received as information. The 2027 financial plan had not been presented by Nov 7, 2026.
figures: Taxable assessment +9% ($131M); residential +12%; commercial/industrial +5%; province +11% ($12.1B) (Jun 16, 2026 0:17:02-0:19:41); average single-family +3.0%, apartment unit +3.1%, condominium -0.2% (minutes Jun 16, 2026, item 15).
notes: The assessor is a provincial official making a presentation; identified by initials as a delegation.
